World.title: PM Magyar says Hungary enters ‘one of the worst energy crises in decades’, shares new Paks shutdown date
World.content:
Hungary is entering what Prime Minister Péter Magyar has described as one of the country’s most serious energy crises in decades, with the most critical period expected to begin on Monday as the Paks Nuclear Power Plant moves closer to a possible full shutdown.

Speaking at two emergency press briefings on Friday (first at MOL’s Danube Refinery in Százhalombatta and later at the Paks Nuclear Power Plant), the prime minister outlined the government’s response to the unprecedented situation created by the Danube’s exceptionally low water level.

Paks could stop generating electricity next week

Magyar said the nuclear power station is currently operating at roughly 960 megawatts, less than half of its normal 2,000-megawatt capacity.

According to the government, the Danube stood at minus 124 centimetres on Friday, while the plant’s final operating reactor must be shut down if the river falls to minus 134 centimetres to comply with safety regulations.

Based on the latest forecasts, the final reactor may have to be taken offline on Tuesday or Wednesday, although Magyar warned that the country’s most difficult period is expected to begin as early as Monday.

The prime minister stressed repeatedly that the situation does not pose a nuclear safety risk. He said the shutdown procedure follows long-established safety protocols, while the reactors’ cooling systems will continue operating even after electricity generation stops.

Long shutdown possible as drought continues

Officials warned that the outage could last longer than initially expected. Current weather forecasts indicate little chance of significant rainfall across the Danube catchment area in the coming weeks, meaning water levels may remain below the threshold required to restart the reactors.

The government said experts are continuously monitoring the river, with emergency mobile pumps available if the water level falls further to ensure cooling water can still be supplied safely.

Government seeks to avoid blackouts

Magyar said the government’s top priority is preventing nationwide power outages. He urged Hungary’s largest industrial consumers to cut electricity usage, particularly between 5 PM and 10 PM, when demand is highest.

According to the prime minister, Thursday evening’s peak electricity demand was already 151 megawatts lower than forecast thanks to voluntary reductions, while MOL has committed to reducing its own electricity consumption by 65 megawatts.

Meanwhile, the Dunamenti Power Plant is expected to begin trial operations on Saturday after repairs, with around 400 megawatts of generating capacity scheduled to return by Sunday.

Photo: MTI

PM blames previous governments

Magyar argued that the current situation has been made worse by years of insufficient investment. He claimed the previous government failed to upgrade Paks after the Danube reached a record low in 2018, despite improvements being carried out at the Dunamenti Power Plant, where modifications to the water intake system have allowed operations to continue despite the current drought.

According to the prime minister, the temporary loss of Paks’ electricity production could cost the state budget around HUF 50 billion per month. He also criticised what he described as misinformation surrounding the crisis, urging political actors not to spread false claims or create unnecessary panic.

Climate change and energy policy under scrutiny

Magyar said the crisis illustrates how unprepared Hungary has been for the effects of climate change. He criticised previous governments for failing to accelerate investments in wind power, electricity storage and other renewable energy technologies, arguing that a more diversified energy system would have reduced the country’s dependence on both Russian technology and the Danube’s water level.

The government has already approved plans to allow the construction of new wind farms with a combined capacity roughly double that of the current Paks Nuclear Power Plant, he said.

If you missed it: Thousands lose water supply in Hungary as Paks output is cut and red warnings are issued

Emergency task force considers further measures

An emergency government defence task force was scheduled to meet on Friday evening to examine several contingency plans in case Paks is forced to shut down completely. Among the options under consideration is the possibility of restricting certain rail freight operations during peak demand periods to reduce pressure on the electricity grid.

The government is also assessing the availability of additional electricity imports from neighbouring countries to help maintain supply if domestic generation falls further.

Subscribe to receive every edition of our Hungary Insider newsletter directly in your inbox!

PM dismisses rumours over Danube and Ukraine

Magyar also rejected social media claims that neighbouring countries, including Austria, Germany and Slovakia, were deliberately withholding water from the Danube. According to the prime minister, neither the government nor Hungary’s water management authorities have found any evidence to support those allegations.

He likewise denied reports that Hungary is exporting electricity to Ukraine during the current energy crisis, saying the opposite is true in the present circumstances.

World.title: Hungary convenes emergency task force as heatwave puts water and energy systems under pressure
World.content:
The Hungarian government has convened an emergency meeting of its defence task force to address growing concerns over the country’s water and energy systems as an intense heatwave continues to grip Hungary. Prime Minister Péter Magyar said key decisions would be taken on Friday evening following consultations with ministers, infrastructure operators and regulators.

Emergency meeting to address water and energy challenges

Speaking at a press conference at MOL’s Danube Refinery in Százhalombatta, Magyar said the government would hold an emergency session of its defence task force on Friday evening to decide on the most urgent measures needed to respond to the developing situation.

According to the prime minister, the task force brings together members of the government, representatives of regulatory authorities, public agencies and the operators of Hungary’s critical infrastructure.

Before the meeting, Magyar said he would continue consultations with ministers, regulators and infrastructure leaders, including further discussions in Paks, where the government has been monitoring the impact of the Danube’s exceptionally low water level on the country’s energy supply. The government said it would announce the decisions taken after the meeting.

Government appeals for greater public cooperation

Magyar said Hungary’s water utility companies had prepared extensively for the heatwave and the increased demand for drinking water. However, he warned that many households were still ignoring official requests to reduce water consumption.

According to the prime minister, some residents have continued watering gardens and filling swimming pools despite repeated appeals to conserve water. He urged the public to avoid these activities over the coming days in order to help maintain a stable drinking water supply, describing uninterrupted water service as the government’s highest priority.

Companies asked to cut energy consumption further

The prime minister also renewed his appeal for voluntary energy-saving measures, particularly among large industrial consumers. He praised companies that have already announced reductions in electricity use, citing Samsung and the Budapest Municipality as examples. At the same time, he encouraged businesses to go even further.

“I ask companies to multiply those figures by two or three before sending us the email,” Magyar said, referring to the voluntary energy-saving commitments submitted to the government.

Subscribe to receive every edition of our Hungary Insider newsletter directly in your inbox!

“We have the situation under control”

Despite the mounting pressure caused by the prolonged heatwave, Magyar sought to reassure the public. “We have the situation under control, and it can remain under control,” he said. At the same time, he cautioned that the current period of extreme weather could last not only for several days but potentially for weeks. To minimise disruption and damage, he said, genuine cooperation between the government, businesses and the public would be essential.

World.title: Hungary population decline continues: country loses tens of thousands of people in 6 months
World.content:
Hungary’s population continued to decline during the first half of 2026, with births once again significantly outnumbered by deaths, according to the latest preliminary figures published by the Hungarian Central Statistical Office (KSH). While both the number of births and deaths fell compared with a year earlier, the country still recorded a natural population decrease of more than 28,000 people in the first six months of the year.

Fewer births and deaths in June

According to KSH, 5,790 children were born in June 2026, down 2.6% (157 births) from June last year. During the same month, 9,167 people died, representing a 3.1% decrease (291 fewer deaths) compared with June 2025.

As a result, Hungary’s natural population decline—the difference between births and deaths—stood at 3,377 people in June, slightly lower than the 3,511 recorded in the same month a year earlier. The number of marriages, however, increased. 4,942 couples married in June, up 8.9% year-on-year.

Population fell by more than 28,000 in first half of the year

According to KSH figures, between January and June 2026, a total of 34,312 children were born, 2.0% fewer than during the same period in 2025. Over the same six months, 62,330 people died, a 4.1% decrease compared with the previous year.

Despite the lower mortality rate, deaths continued to far exceed births, resulting in a natural population decline of 28,018 people. Although still substantial, this was 6.6% lower than the 29,994 recorded during the first half of 2025.

Fertility rate remains low

The figures also show that Hungary’s total fertility rate remained largely unchanged at 1.27 children per woman, slightly below last year’s 1.28.

During the first half of the year, there were 7.3 live births and 13.3 deaths per 1,000 inhabitants. The infant mortality rate stood at 4.1 deaths per 1,000 live births, marginally higher than a year earlier.

Marriages continue to rise

Marriage numbers were one of the few positive demographic indicators. A total of 21,177 couples married between January and June, an increase of 4.4% (895 marriages) compared with the same period in 2025.

On a rolling 12-month basis, from July 2025 to June 2026, 47,477 couples married, also marking a 4.0% increase over the previous 12 months.

Subscribe to receive every edition of our Hungary Insider newsletter directly in your inbox!

Regional differences

The demographic trends varied across Hungary. Births declined in Budapest and three other regions but increased in four regions, with the strongest growth recorded in Northern Hungary. Budapest experienced the largest decline in births.

Deaths fell in every region except the Northern Great Plain, while the natural population decrease improved across all regions except Budapest. Marriage numbers increased in every region outside the capital, with Northern Hungary recording the strongest growth.

Although mortality continued to decline, the latest figures underline that Hungary’s long-term demographic challenges remain. The number of births is still well below the number of deaths, meaning the country’s population continues to shrink despite modest improvements in some indicators.

World.title: Man in custody after attacking train conductor on Budapest-Vienna service
World.content:
A Hungarian court has ordered the pre-trial detention of a man accused of violently attacking a train conductor on a Budapest–Vienna service, before allegedly threatening to kill the railway employee and resisting police officers at Komárom railway station.

The Tatabánya District Court ordered the suspect to remain in custody for one month on suspicion of committing violence against a person performing public duties, according to a statement issued by the court.

Alleged assault began during ticket inspection

Prosecutors say the incident took place on 28 July, when the man was travelling on a train from Budapest to Vienna.

According to the investigation, the conductor asked the passenger to present his ticket. The suspect was reportedly talking to himself before suddenly standing up and striking the conductor forcefully on the head and chest without any apparent provocation.

The conductor retreated into the train corridor, but investigators say the man followed him and repeatedly punched him across the body.

Emergency stop at Komárom

The train came to an emergency stop at Komárom railway station, where the suspect allegedly continued behaving aggressively.

According to the court, he threatened to kill the conductor even after the train had stopped.

When police officers arrived at the scene, the man reportedly shouted aggressively at them and refused repeated instructions to comply. Officers eventually restrained and handcuffed him using physical force.

Subscribe to receive every edition of our Hungary Insider newsletter directly in your inbox!

Court cites flight risk and witness intimidation concerns

The court ruled that the legal conditions for pre-trial detention had been met because the offence carries a potential prison sentence. Judges also found there was a genuine risk that the suspect could flee or go into hiding. According to the court, there are indications that he intended to leave Hungary for an unknown destination before his arrest.

In addition, the court said there were reasonable grounds to believe that, if released, the suspect could intimidate or unlawfully influence witnesses who have yet to be questioned during the criminal proceedings. For these reasons, the court ordered his detention for one month. The decision is final.

World.title: Critical situation: PM Magyar and MOL CEO on Hungary’s fuel supplies, Russian oil, power station and tourist boats
World.content:
Hungary is preparing for a critical period in its energy system after Prime Minister Péter Magyar announced that the Paks Nuclear Power Plant is expected to be shut down from Monday due to the Danube’s exceptionally low water level. Speaking alongside MOL Chairman and CEO Zsolt Hernádi on Friday, the prime minister urged households and businesses to reduce electricity consumption as the country prepares for the unprecedented disruption.

Paks shutdown expected as Danube reaches critical levels

At an extraordinary press briefing held at MOL’s Danube Refinery in Százhalombatta, Magyar said the situation is likely to become critical from Monday.

The prime minister warned that another reduction in output at the Paks Nuclear Power Plant is expected before the facility is completely taken offline. If this happens, it will mark the first full shutdown in the plant’s 44-year history caused by extremely low water levels in the Danube.

Magyar stressed that the decision is based solely on safety considerations and urged former Fidesz politicians to stop spreading what he described as misinformation suggesting the shutdown is unnecessary.

“Experts are not making these decisions lightly,” he said.

According to the prime minister, a full shutdown of Paks would result in an estimated HUF 50 billion loss per month for the Hungarian economy.

Government urges households and businesses to save electricity

Magyar highlighted that electricity demand peaks each day between 5 PM and 10 PM, calling on the public to reduce consumption during those hours whenever possible.

He also appealed to Hungary’s largest industrial energy users to cut their electricity use in preparation for Monday’s expected supply pressures.

The prime minister announced that MOL itself will reduce its energy consumption by 40%, adding that the government will provide the company with additional assistance to ensure the continued operation of critical fuel infrastructure.

Photo: MTI

Magyar: The ships and barges are stuck

“The ships are stuck—not just the tourist boats; even the barges can’t come in, and we can’t cool Paks,” Magyar listed some pressing problems. However, he said that in other European countries, it is possible to navigate the Danube. According to the prime minister, experts need to be brought in because the problem isn’t going to go away: it needs to be solved.

MOL: Hungary has sufficient fuel supplies

Speaking alongside the prime minister, Zsolt Hernádi, Chairman and CEO of MOL, sought to reassure the public that Hungary has adequate fuel reserves.

“There is enough fuel in Hungary,” he said, while acknowledging that the exceptionally low level of the Danube has created operational challenges for the country’s largest refinery.

Hernádi revealed that MOL had requested government assistance because of the critically low river level affecting logistics and refinery operations.

He also said the company is continuing preparations to reduce its dependence on Russian crude oil ahead of legislative changes due to take effect next year. However, he noted that uncertainty remains over the future capacity of the Adriatic Pipeline, making close cooperation with the government essential.

Asked about fuel prices, Hernádi declined to comment, saying any statement could influence the market. Magyar jokingly interrupted by saying, “I’ll talk about it,” prompting laughter as Hernádi replied that he could not stop the prime minister from doing so.

Danube power station returns to full capacity

Magyar also announced that the Dunamenti Power Plant is expected to return to full capacity on Saturday after the arrival of a replacement component, providing additional support to Hungary’s electricity system ahead of the expected Paks shutdown.

Government monitors water infrastructure

Beyond the energy sector, the prime minister warned that Hungary’s ageing water infrastructure is under increasing strain because of the prolonged heatwave and drought.

He said burst water mains are likely in the coming days, arguing that decades of underinvestment by previous governments have left the network vulnerable during periods of extreme demand.

Magyar added that the heads of Hungary’s critical infrastructure operators had been summoned for an emergency meeting later on Friday.

Subscribe to receive every edition of our Hungary Insider newsletter directly in your inbox!

Hungary seeks regional cooperation over the Danube

The government is also looking beyond Hungary’s borders in response to the worsening drought.

Magyar said he had instructed Foreign Minister Anita Orbán to contact her counterparts in neighbouring countries to explore possible regional cooperation aimed at addressing the Danube’s rapidly falling water level.

While he did not outline specific measures, the move reflects growing concern over the impact of the prolonged drought on energy production, water supplies and transport across Central Europe.

World.title: Nscale to acquire Romanian co-founded AI startup Anyscale in reportedly USD 1.65 billion deal
World.content:
Cloud infrastructure provider Nscale will acquire AI software startup Anyscale, which has Romanian-born university professor Ion Stoica among its co-founders, in a transaction worth roughly USD 1.65 billion, according to a Bloomberg News source.

Ion Stoica is a co-founder of Anyscale, together with Robert Nishihara (chief executive officer) and Philipp Moritz (chief technology officer), who were his PhD students at RISELab within the University of California, Berkeley.

San Francisco-based Anyscale provides software for organizing and managing complex AI workloads so that they can run smoothly across multiple computers simultaneously. Nscale said it expects to attract more customers by offering Anyscale’s software.

Anyscale will continue to operate under its own brand and serve its existing customers, the companies said. Anyscale’s entire team of approximately 200 people across the United States, Europe and India will join Nscale as part of the acquisition.

The transaction is expected to be completed in the second half of this year, the companies said.

Anyscale recorded revenue growth of 70% compared with the previous quarter in the company’s most recent quarter, according to a blog post by its co-founders.

Originally from Romania, Stoica left for the United States in the late 1990s to pursue his PhD at Carnegie Mellon University. Since 2000, he has been teaching at UC Berkeley, where he leads a laboratory funded largely by technology companies such as Microsoft, Nvidia, Google, and IBM, with an annual budget of more than USD 6 million.

Stoica became a billionaire by launching four startups that originated from his research laboratory at the University of California, Berkeley. World.title: UNICEF, Romanian Labor Ministry launch e-Learning HUB for professionals in social assistance
World.content:
Romania’s Labor Ministry and UNICEF announced the launch of e-Learning HUB, a national platform dedicated to the continuous professional training of personnel in the field of social services and sectors that contribute to social inclusion.

The HUB provides coordinated access to training opportunities, educational resources and professional development programs. The platform brings together continuous professional training opportunities for specialists in the social field, covering essential topics such as the protection of vulnerable persons, human rights, digital skills and quality standards in social services.

The HUB is designed to become the digital foundation of the future National Center for Continuous Training in Social Assistance, which is scheduled to become operational in 2028. The platform will contribute to increasing the skills of professionals in social assistance and related fields, personnel of central and local public authorities with responsibilities in the social field, decision-makers, accredited professional training providers, professional organizations, and non-governmental organizations active in the field of social assistance and the protection of human rights.

“Through e-Learning HUB, specialists across the country will be able to identify relevant courses more easily, develop their skills and have access to modern resources adapted to the real needs of the system,” said Silvia Dinică, State Secretary within the Labor Ministry.

“Professionals in social services are facing increasingly complex challenges, from poverty and social exclusion to the effects of recent crises on children and families. The e-Learning HUB platform offers a single access point to quality learning opportunities and represents an important step toward strengthening the workforce in the social field,” said Anna Riatti, UNICEF Representative in Romania.

The e-Learning HUB will facilitate access to accredited training programs, promote collaboration between institutions and training providers, and support the development of the skills needed to provide integrated and quality services.

World.title: Bucharest Community Foundation and City Hall begin transforming Herăstrău Park through public-private collaboration
World.content:
Bucharest City Hall and the Bucharest Community Foundation announced on Friday, July 31, that they have begun transforming the city’s major northern park, Herăstrău, according to the priorities expressed by nearly 10,000 participants in the public consultation.

The process benefits from private funding worth EUR 900,000 already mobilized by the Bucharest Community Foundation. The first EUR 90,000 will be invested in the studies and expertise required for the regeneration of the park’s green spaces, with the remainder to be directed as the stages are established together with the public administration.

The funds will cover the tree inventory through a TreePlotter-type digital application, the creation of a public inventory, specialized studies, technical and dendrological expertise, assessment of tree health and risk, preparation of the tree management plan, as well as the documentation needed to establish design requirements for future interventions.

The digital tree inventory will be public and accessible both to the administration and citizens and will form the basis of a Green Register dedicated to Old Herăstrău Park. For each tree, GIS location, dendrometric characteristics, health status, and management recommendations will be recorded. Data can be permanently updated by the public administration, and the tool can be gradually expanded to the entire Herăstrău Park, providing a permanent instrument for monitoring and adaptive and sustainable management of tree heritage.

The two partners began working together through a new collaboration model that brings together public administration, the community, specialists and private funders. The new working mechanism allows preparatory stages to begin quickly, independently of the public budget calendar, while maintaining decision-making, control and ownership of the documentation within the public administration.

The Bucharest Community Foundation will finance and contract specialists for the regeneration of green spaces based on specifications agreed with the authorities and experts involved, while the results will be handed over to the Bucharest City Hall and will serve as the basis for future design and construction works.

Meanwhile, the two partners will prepare the administrative framework for major interventions and mobilize the private sector and civil society to attract the financial resources necessary for the subsequent stages of the regeneration process. Private resources will accelerate project preparation without transferring decision-making rights over the park to funders. Control, validation and ownership of documentation will remain the responsibility of the public administration, while intervention solutions and priorities will be defined in collaboration with specialists, funders and community members, in accordance with the principles of the New European Bauhaus.

Going forward, the Bucharest Community Foundation aims to attract funds of up to EUR 10 million from the private sector and civil society for the subsequent intervention plan.

“If we waited for the completion of administrative procedures for landscape design, as well as for securing the lakeside area, we would not have enough speed. That is why I cannot sufficiently emphasize the role of the Bucharest Community Foundation. My role was to be open to collaboration and, together, to create this mechanism through which we can get on track, set things in motion, and accelerate interventions,” said Bucharest mayor Ciprian Ciucu.

Public consultation

The planned works follow a public consultation carried out between May and June 2026, in which nearly half of respondents said that they were dissatisfied with the current state of the park.

Participants’ expectations were very concrete. Modernization of general infrastructure was considered a priority by 83.2% of respondents, while 74.3% indicated the restoration of the natural environment as one of the main intervention directions. Permanent public toilets, more numerous and cleaner, represented the most requested specific measure resulting from the consultation, indicated by 85.5% of respondents. Better lighting at night was desired by 81.4% of respondents, followed by the rehabilitation of paths and paving (77.9%), ensuring functional drinking fountains (68.9%) and improving urban furniture (61.6%).

Restoring the natural environment was equally important. Among the respondents, 78.6% requested more trees and denser vegetation for shade, cooling and air filtration, while 71.2% wanted improved lake water quality, and 56.9% wanted better access to the waterfront. Nearly half of participants mentioned degraded paths and sidewalks among the main complaints, while responses indicate a clear preference for preserving the park’s natural character and avoiding excessive interventions.

World.title: Over 6 in 10 Romanians cannot afford a one-week annual vacation
World.content:
Romania ranks first in the European Union in terms of the share of people who cannot afford a one-week annual vacation away from home, according to data published by Eurostat on Thursday, July 30.

According to the European Statistical Office, 61.4% of Romanians aged 16 or older said they could not afford a one-week vacation away from home in 2025. Romania is followed by Greece, where 46.6% of residents were in the same situation, and by Bulgaria and Hungary, both with 39.1%.

The difference from the European Union average is significant. Across the 27 member states, 27.5% of people aged over 16 said they could not afford a one-week holiday away from home.

Compared with 2024, the share of people who cannot afford a vacation increased by 0.5% across the European Union. However, the long-term trend remains positive. Compared with 2015, the indicator has fallen by 7.7%, so over the last decade more and more Europeans have gained the financial ability to go on holiday for at least one week a year.

At the other end of the ranking are the states where an annual vacation is accessible to the vast majority of the population. The lowest share of people unable to afford a one-week holiday was recorded in Luxembourg, where only 10.6% of residents said they could not cover such an expense. It is followed by Sweden, with 12.4%, and the Netherlands, with 12.8%, values almost five times lower than those reported in Romania.

The ability to spend at least one week a year on vacation away from home is one of the indicators used by Eurostat to assess living conditions and the level of material deprivation in the member states. The data highlight the persistent differences between European economies in terms of purchasing power and households’ ability to cover expenses considered normal for a decent standard of living.

World.title: Romania launches national campaign to promote its 13 national parks
World.content:
The Ministry of Environment and the Conservation Carpathia Foundation have launched a nationwide campaign to promote Romania’s 13 national parks and raise public awareness about their environmental and economic value. The campaign, titled Parks for Generations (Parcurile Generațiilor), was launched during the Făgăraș Fest festival and will run on television, radio, and digital platforms.

The initiative seeks to explain the difference between national parks and other natural or urban parks, encouraging Romanians to visit the protected areas while highlighting their role in biodiversity conservation, climate resilience, and local development.

Romania's 13 national parks protect around 317,500 hectares of land, including forests, alpine meadows, gorges, and caves that provide habitats for numerous rare plant and animal species. According to Conservation Carpathia, the parks also help regulate water cycles, reduce the risks of droughts and floods, and support local economies through tourism-related activities.

The national parks are Buila-Vânturarița, Călimani, Ceahlău, Bicaz Gorges-Hășmaș, Nera Gorges-Beușnița, Cozia, Jiu Gorge, Domogled-Cerna Valley, Măcin Mountains, Rodna Mountains, Piatra Craiului, Retezat, and Semenic-Caraș Gorges.

The campaign follows research showing that public understanding of national parks remains limited. A 2024 study by Unlock Market Research found that while 67% of Romanians said they had visited a national park, many confused them with nature reserves, natural parks, or other protected areas. Another finding showed that 82% of respondents could not define what distinguishes a national park from other forms of nature protection.

“National parks are among the most remarkable places Romania has. They protect nature, but they also create opportunities for local communities and future generations," said Barbara and Christoph Promberger, executive directors of the Conservation Carpathia Foundation.

“We want more Romanians to discover them, understand their value and be proud that Romania has such a rich natural heritage. People protect what they know and appreciate, and that is the first step we want to take together," they added.

In her turn, interim environment minister Diana Buzoianu said the campaign aims to address the public's limited knowledge of Romania’s protected areas.

“Romania has national parks with almost a century of history. […] Yet recent data show that too few Romanians know what a national park really is and the role it plays for nature, climate, water, local communities, and the economy," the minister said.

“The Parks for Generations campaign does exactly this: it brings national parks closer to the public and explains, in accessible language, why these places are so important for Romania," she added.

The campaign includes a dedicated online platform featuring information about all 13 national parks, visitor recommendations, and links to each park's official website. It was developed by creative agency Pastel for the Conservation Carpathia Foundation and the Ministry of Environment, with support from the Romanian Rangers Association.

The Conservation Carpathia Foundation is one of Europe's largest private nature conservation initiatives, working to restore ecosystems in Romania's Southern Carpathian Mountains. Since its establishment in 2009, the foundation has acquired more than 28,000 hectares of forests and alpine meadows for conservation, planted over 4.5 million trees on nearly 2,000 hectares of degraded land, and created a 78,000-hectare no-hunting zone.

Its long-term goal is to support the creation of the Făgăraș Mountains National Park, while promoting biodiversity conservation alongside sustainable economic development for local communities.

World.title: Canada’s Alimentation Couche-Tard to acquire controlling stake in Polish Żabka Group, owner of Froo stores in Romania
World.content:
Alimentation Couche-Tard Inc. (TSX: ATD) announced that it plans to acquire a controlling stake in Poland's largest convenience retailer Żabka Group (WSE: ZAB) in a deal valued at USD 8.6 billion.

Couche-Tard will initiate a voluntary tender offer through its wholly owned subsidiary, Circle K Polska sp. z.o.o. for PLN 32.00 (equivalent of USD 8.48) per share, representing a total equity value of approximately PLN 32.62 billion (equivalent of USD 8.6 billion).

The transaction represents the largest acquisition in Couche-Tard’s history, the company said.

The deal is supported by Żabka's key executive managers and shareholders owning, in aggregate, approximately 57% of Żabka's issued and outstanding shares, including CVC Capital Partners and Partners Group.

For Couche-Tard, the acquisition will add an immediate, scaled platform in Central and Eastern Europe, it said.

The Canadian company plans to preserve Żabka's management structure, brand, entrepreneurial franchise model and local expertise.

Couche-Tard expects to fund the transaction through fully committed debt facilities underwritten by J.P. Morgan as Lead Arranger, with National Bank of Canada Capital Markets and The Bank of Nova Scotia acting as Joint Bookrunners.

The transaction is subject to receipt of regulatory approvals, including merger control approval by the European Commission or Polish Prezes Urzędu Konkurencji i Konsumentów (UOKiK), foreign direct investment approval by Romanian Comisia pentru examinarea investiţiilor străine directe, and approval under the European Union's Foreign Subsidies Regulation by the European Commission.

If Couche-Tard reaches at least 95% of the total voting rights in Żabka, it intends to initiate a compulsory acquisition (squeeze-out) of the remaining shares and take the necessary steps to procure the delisting of Żabka's shares from the Warsaw Stock Exchange.

Founded in 1998 and listed on the Warsaw Stock Exchange since October 2024, Żabka Group operates more than 13,000 convenience stores across Poland and Romania and services approximately 4.3 million average daily transactions. Its network is built around compact, modular neighborhood stores averaging approximately 65 sqm, located across urban, suburban and rural communities to serve immediate consumption and everyday convenience needs.

Zabka is present in Romania with a network of stores opened under the brand Froo, which it launched locally in 2024.

The company opened 778 new stores across Poland and Romania in the first half of 2026, including 706 in Poland and 72 in Romania, bringing the total to 13,063 stores at end-June 2026, up 10.8% YoY. In Q2, the group opened 343 new stores, including 303 in Poland and 40 in Romania.

World.title: Croatia’s War Crimes Prosecutions are Stagnating, Watchdog Warns
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Bos/Hrv/Srp

Bozica Ciboci, Vesna Terselic and Veselinka Kastratovic. Photo: Documenta

Since Croatia joined the European Union, the effectiveness of its war-crimes prosecutions has stagnated while crimes committed against Serbian civilians and prisoners-of-war are almost never investigated, a report presented on Friday by Documenta – the Centre for Dealing with the Past, says.

“The number of proceedings is declining. We have recorded 33 criminal proceedings in the trial phase before county courts, involving a total of 91 defendants,” Documenta head Vesna Terselic said, presenting the 2025 Report on Monitoring Criminal Proceedings for War Crimes.

By comparison, there were 54 criminal proceedings in 2024, 64 the year before, and 61 in 2022.

Of the 91 defendants in war-crimes proceedings in 2025, 87 were members of Serbian paramilitary and police forces. The remaining defendants included three former members of the Croatian Army and one member of the Croatian Defence Council, HVO.

Terselic said many dedicated professionals work in the State Attorney’s Office, the police, the courts and the Ministry of Croatian Veterans, but that county state attorneys’ offices lack the capacity to investigate unresolved war-crimes cases.

“Recently, a final verdict brought to an end one of the longest war crimes trials, in which Branimir Glavas was convicted. That trial would not have happened if witness Krunoslav Fehir had not spoken out. It would not have happened if Vladimir Faber had not investigated the case while serving in the police. It was an extremely difficult crime to investigate, and many institutions failed to support the investigation,” Terselic recalled.

She said recent legislative amendments had improved the position of civilian victims of the 1990s Homeland War, but that changes to the law on the rights of victims of sexual violence during the armed aggression against Croatia were still needed.

“Unfortunately, today, there is not a single active trial for crimes committed during Operations Storm and Operation Flash. No one disputes the right of the Croatian Army and police to liberate occupied parts of Croatia and re-establish state authority there, but no one gave them the right to follow that with criminal acts,” said Veselinka Kastratovic, legal adviser at the Centre for Peace, Nonviolence and Human Rights Osijek.

“We cannot say it did not happen. We all know in Croatia that it happened; some people simply choose to look away,” she added.

Documenta’s report also criticises public statements by some high state officials, saying they reflect “one-sided and simplified interpretations of recent history”.

More positively, the report highlighted the commemoration of the killings in Varivode, where then-President Ivo Josipovic and Prime Minister Andrej Plenkovic delivered messages of remembrance.

In Varivode, Croatian soldiers killed nine elderly Serb civilians after Operation Storm, a key Croatian Army operation in 1995, which overwhelmed a self-proclaimed Serbian statelet on Croatian territory.

Bozica Ciboci of Documenta called on countries across the region to “sign agreements aimed at improving the prosecution of war-crimes perpetrators and preventing the politicisation of war crimes trials.”

World.title: Money the Greatest Challenge Facing Serbia’s Small, Independent Media
World.content:
For Serbia’s small independent newsrooms, pressure comes not only in the form of intimidation, spurious lawsuits, or physical assault. Increasingly, it is financial.

The Serbian media landscape is sharply divided between outlets close to the ruling Serbian Progressive Party, SNS, and independent newsrooms.

Research has found that media loyal to the ruling party are the primary beneficiaries of co-financing and advertising from public bodies. Independent media are starved of such funds.

This helps explain why pro-government outlets can operate without the same financial pressures, while independent newsrooms struggle to cover basic overheads and remain vulnerable to political and economic pressure.

World.title: Democracy Digest: Danube Falls to Lowest Levels in 30 Years
World.content:
Suspected Russian missile lands in Poland; extradition of former justice minister sought

A cruise missile crossed into eastern Poland early on Thursday, striking a field and apparently exploding on impact, during another large-scale Russian attack on Ukraine. Poland’s Operational Command said radar detected an unidentified object moving west at 03:40 and dispatched an F-16 to identify and intercept it. Six minutes later, the object disappeared from radar. A Mi-24 helicopter traced its probable impact point to an uninhabited area near Tarnawa-Kolonia in Lublin province. Police arriving at the site found fragments spread around a crater approximately 10 metres across, some 2 kilometres from the nearest homes. No one was injured and no buildings were damaged. The area was checked for explosive and radiological hazards before investigators began examining it. Speaking to reporters, PM Donald Tusk said the preliminary evidence pointed to a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile, but stressed that this still had to be confirmed. He said there was no reason to believe Poland had been the intended target, and that Polish forces were prepared to shoot the missile down had it continued flying. “This war is full of surprises, and we must learn very quickly from new situations and possible new threats,” Tusk said. “For now, the reports – particularly the military ones – indicate that everything worked as it should.” Maksymilian Dura, a retired naval commander and Defence24 expert, said it was possible that the Russians had deliberately directed the missile over Poland. “Given Russia’s desperation and the difficult situation it is now in, they may simply be probing us. Such incidents will happen again,” he told PAP. The episode adds to a growing record of the war crossing Poland’s border. In September 2025, 19 Russian drones entered Polish airspace in a single night, prompting allied NATO aircraft to intervene.

Poland this week formally requested the US detain and extradite former justice minister Zbigniew Ziobro, who is wanted over alleged abuses of the Justice Fund under the previous Law and Justice government. Spokeswoman for the National Prosecutor’s Office Anna Adamiak said the request, submitted through diplomatic channels on Monday, covers 19 of the 26 offences prosecutors have attributed to Ziobro. Prosecutors accuse him of directing a criminal group, exceeding his powers and steering grants towards selected organisations. Ziobro, in the US since May, has not been questioned in the investigation and denies fleeing Poland. He had previously received protection in Hungary, but the new government there later withdrew his refugee status and invalidated his travel documents. The US Justice Department will first assess whether Poland’s request meets the treaty’s formal requirements. A federal judge would then rule on whether extradition is legally permissible, before the final decision passes to the US secretary of state. Polish prosecutors say the process could take anywhere from several months to several years. Responding on X, the former justice minister said he trusted the independence of American institutions and expected them to examine what he called the case’s political context. “Donald Tusk, Adam Bodnar and Waldemar Zurek repeatedly publicly prejudged my guilt before any independent court had examined the case,” he claimed.

World.title: Bosnia’s Mainly Serb Entity Ramps Up Lobbying Outlay under Trump
World.content:
In 2021, under the Democrat administration of President Joe Biden, lobbyists hired by the Republika Srpska authorities were focussed mainly on forwarding messages from Banja Luka to US senators, including Marco Rubio, now US Secretary of State.

In early 2022, however, the focus shifted to direct conversations with, for example, Robin Brooks, the then director of the Department of Human Rights and Humanitarian Affairs at the US State Department and Republican congressman Robert Aderholt.

“Our goal is a network of relevant interlocutors who share key principles: respect for Dayton, appreciation of reality, and readiness for rational cooperation,” said Ana Trisic Babic, director of the Office for International Cooperation of the Republika Srpska.

Trump’s return to office in January 2025 brought a significant hike in spending by the Republika Srpska in the US. Since then, the entity has hired four new lobbying firms: Zell & Associates International Advocates, Stokes Strategies, GS2Law and Continental Strategy.

Zell & Associates International Advocates was paid around a million euros, though almost half of that went to an Israeli subcontractor called Gilad Government Relations and Lobbying.

One of the most influential lobbying firms in Israel, Gilad is co-owned by Ariel Sender, who headed Trump’s campaign among US citizens in Israel during the 2016 and 2020 elections; in 2012, the Israeli parliament, or Knesset, temporarily revoked the entry passes for Gilad staff amid an ethics scandal.

Zell & Associates did not respond to a request for comment.

Republika Srpska also paid around half a million euros to Stokes Strategies, whose submissions to FARA show it focussed on building relations with conservative organisations and meetings in Congress.

Stokes paid Christine Czerjenewski of Firefly Communications some 50,000 euros for research work. Czerjenewski has connections in US conservative circles and the Republican Party and is a former fellow of the conservative public policy group The Heritage Foundation, described by The New York Times this week as a “bastion of American conservatism”.

Neither Stokes Strategies nor Firefly Communications responded to requests for comment.

A month before the US lifted sanctions on Dodik & Co, Republika Srpska authorities hired GS2Law to the tune of 130,000 euros.

According to their FARA report, GS2Law was tasked with legal research and preparation of a lawsuit “in connection with the previous listing of certain citizens and entities of Republika Srpska on the OFAC [sanctions] list”.

GS2Law did not respond to a request for comment.

Continental Strategy was hired earlier this year, on a contract worth around 660,000 euros. The firm is led by former Trump adviser Carlos Trujillo.

World.title: Serbian Feminists Expect Boost From Montenegro’s Menstrual Leave Law
World.content:
Serbian women’s rights organisations say they feel encouraged by developments in neighbouring Montenegro, which has adopted law changes introducing two paid days of “menstrual leave” per month for women diagnosed with secondary dysmenorrhea, or severe menstrual cramp.

“It has generated considerable enthusiasm among women. It feels like a very progressive idea and a major step forward, especially if we take into account that no country in the wider region has a law introducing such measures,” said Ljiljana Todorovic Jovanovic, founder of the FemIn Collective, a women’s rights NGO from Pozarevac.

The news from Montenegro has been hailed by Serbian women’s rights groups but criticised by some of the general public, activists said.

“Part of the general public welcomed the move and expressed hope that something similar would be introduced in Serbia. However, another part interpreted the news as meaning that women had been granted some kind of privilege,” Ana Mirkailo, an activist from Befem, a Belgrade-based feminist cultural centre and NGO founded in 2009, told BIRN.

She added that this divided reaction didn’t surprise her but “served as a reminder of how much work still needs to be done in this area”.

Spain was the first country in Europe to introduce paid “menstrual leave” in 2023, followed by Portugal, which has allowed up to three consecutive paid days off per month since 2025 for people experiencing disabling pain caused by diagnosed endometriosis or adenomyosis.

The Montenegrin measure applies to women suffering from serious conditions such as endometriosis, uterine fibroids, endometrial polyps, ovarian inflammation and polycystic ovary syndrome.

According to the explanatory note accompanying the legislation, the amendments are intended to properly regulate diagnosed pathological conditions, eliminate prejudice against women in the workplace, and help balance their health needs with professional obligations.

Todorovic Jovanovic said women in Serbia with menstrual health problems can already take ordinary sick leave, during which they receive 65 per cent of their salary. The problem, however, is that employers do not always respond well when employees request sick leave.

“On paper, the law allows workers to take sick leave simply by visiting a doctor, but there are employers and workplaces where taking leave is effectively impossible – whether to care for a child, because of illness, or due to menstrual health problems,” Todorovic Jovanovic said, adding that even if a similar law as Montenegro’s were adopted, the question of implementation in practice would remain.

For years there have been attempts in Serbia to address menstrual health issues as part of women’s general health, and put them up for discussion.

Last year, a Menstrual Justice Initiative was established in Serbia, bringing together researchers and several women’s organisations from across the country. The initiative was created to advocate for greater recognition of menstrual health and related rights.

The latest law changes in Montenegro have given Menstrual Justice Initiative fresh momentum.

“Women’s organisations actively monitor and listen to the communities they work with, and it is important to respond to that momentum. Legislative initiatives of this kind should originate from women’s organisations and be developed in cooperation with political actors who demonstrate a genuine willingness to support them,” Mirkailo said.

Both Todorovic Jovanovic and Mirkailo agreed that menstrual leave is not a “privilege” and that the question of menstrual leave is not only a question of health but of obtaining work-based rights for those who need them.

Todorovic Jovanovic, from Femin Collective, which is a member of the Menstrual Justice Initiative, explains that two main advocacy models are being pursued in the region. The first focuses on reducing VAT on menstrual products, while the second concerns the introduction of “menstrual leave”, as in Montenegro.

North Macedonia currently has the lowest VAT rate on menstrual products in the region, at 5 per cent, compared with 20 per cent in Serbia and 21 per cent in Montenegro.

“What we have been considering is initially directing our advocacy efforts towards reducing VAT, based on research conducted by the Gender Knowledge Hub, which reported in 2023 that women needed about 8,300 dinars (70 euros) a year to cover the cost of menstrual products,” Todorovic Jovanovic said.

She explained that this becomes particularly significant when it is considered how many women come from socially disadvantaged groups and cannot afford these essential products.

World.title: Live From Manhattan: Bosnia’s Republika Srpska and a Selective View of the Past
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp

In late July, Denis Bojic, the director of the Republika Srpska Memorial Centre, told the Serbian daily newspaper Politika: “The politics of memory is a means of survival.”

Bojic was commenting on the Centre’s recent campaign in New York, in which billboards bearing photographs and accounts testifying to the ‘suffering’ of the Serb people travelled through Manhattan.

Bojic’s words offered perhaps the clearest explanation of the campaign’s political significance. If Republika Srpska, the predominantly Serb-populated entity of Bosnia and Herzegovina, were denied the right to tell the world about Serb suffering, he said, it would mean “the end of the existence of Republika Srpska”.

‘Learn About Serbian Suffering’ was presented in New York on July 10 and 11 by the Memorial Centre, a public institution established by the Republika Srpska government in 2024.

According to the organisers, the exhibition appeared at a number of prominent locations in the city, including near the headquarters of the United Nations. A QR code was displayed, directing interested passers-by to a digital collection of testimonies and archival material.

Even the timing of the exhibition was political.

World.title: Animal Rights Group Calls for End to Breeding at Zagreb Zoo After Lioness’ Death
World.content:
August the 1st, 2026 – A prominent Croatian animal rights group is calling for an end to breeding at Zagreb Zoo following the tragic death of a lioness at the jaws of a male lion just days ago.

Croatian animal welfare organisation Friends of Animals (Prijatelji životinja) has called on the City of Zagreb to end animal breeding at Zagreb Zoo following the death of lioness Tayra, who was killed by the male lion Uganda after the pair were introduced for breeding. The group says the incident should prompt a fundamental review of the zoo’s policies rather than be treated as an isolated accident.

Index reports that in an open appeal to the city, the organisation urged the zoo to stop breeding animals and to end the practice of acquiring, buying, selling, exchanging or gifting animals with other zoos. It argues that Zagreb cannot undo Tayra’s death but can prevent future generations of animals from spending their entire lives in captivity.

The group also opposes reports that the zoo may bring in another lioness to replace Tayra. According to Friends of Animals, a new lioness would likely be introduced for breeding, meaning any cubs born would also spend their lives in captivity. They stress they are not calling for the zoo to close immediately or for existing animals to be relocated, but instead want breeding and the acquisition of new animals to end.

Friends of Animals argue that every new animal born or brought into the zoo extends the cycle of captivity for decades. Instead, they want the City of Zagreb to develop a long-term plan to transform the zoo into an educational, tourist and interactive centre that no longer depends on keeping animals in enclosures.

Their proposal includes replacing live animal exhibits with modern technology such as virtual recreations of natural habitats, interactive museums, 3D projections, holograms, augmented and virtual reality experiences, and live streams from national parks, protected areas and wildlife sanctuaries. The organisation believes these alternatives could educate visitors while avoiding the ethical concerns associated with captivity.

The group says Zagreb has the opportunity to become one of the first cities to begin transforming the traditional zoo model through ethical and technological innovation. It argues that modern education no longer requires cages and that respect for animals cannot be taught while keeping them confined.

Friends of Animals has requested an official response from the City of Zagreb and says Tayra’s death should serve as a warning and a catalyst for changing the long-term direction of Zagreb Zoo.

World.title: INA Confirms Major Natural Gas Potential in the Northern Adriatic
World.content:
August the 1st, 2026 – Croatia’s energy company INA has confirmed a significant new natural gas discovery in the northern Adriatic.

Sinisa Malus reports for Poslovni that this latest discovery fully reinforces previous expectations that the offshore area still holds substantial untapped reserves. It could play a very important role in the country’s future energy supply. The announcement follows the successful completion of the first well in a new multi-year investment programme.

The newly completed Ana-4 DIR well, drilled within an existing northern Adriatic production field, reached a depth of 1,282 metres. Initial testing across three gas-bearing reservoirs produced a combined flow rate of around 160,000 cubic metres of natural gas per day, making it one of INA’s strongest-performing gas wells.

The company said the results confirm that Croatia’s offshore gas fields still contain considerable remaining reserves, despite decades of production. Preparations are now underway to connect the well to the existing production infrastructure so engineers can carry out extended testing, clean the reservoirs and gather additional data needed to certify the reserves and determine long-term production capacity.

The successful well is the first in a five-well drilling campaign that forms part of an investment cycle worth approximately €65 million. Drilling was carried out using the Labin jack-up drilling rig, operated by INA’s subsidiary CROSCO, without any reported safety or environmental incidents.

Work is already moving to the next stage of the programme. The Labin rig is being relocated to the IKA JZ-6 DIR location, where drilling of the second well will begin as INA continues its effort to increase domestic gas production from the northern Adriatic.

INA says the project is strategically important because increasing domestic production strengthens Croatia’s energy security and reduces reliance on imported natural gas. The company believes the northern Adriatic will remain a key source of Croatian gas supplies for years to come, with additional development of offshore reserves planned throughout the investment programme.

World.title: Croatia to Expand Bottle Deposit Scheme in Biggest Overhaul Yet
World.content:
August the 1st, 2026 – Croatia’s deposit return system is set for its biggest expansion since it was introduced, with major changes coming into force from the 1st of January, 2027.

Poslovni reports that consumers will soon be able to return far more than just plastic bottles, glass bottles and cans, as the government plans to include additional types of beverage packaging in the scheme.

Under the new rules, the 10-cent refundable deposit will also apply to multilayer carton packaging, commonly known as Tetra Pak, which is widely used for milk, dairy drinks and fruit juices. In addition, all beverage containers smaller than 200 millilitres, previously excluded from the system, will also be covered. As a result, these products will cost 10 cents more at the checkout, with shoppers receiving the money back when they return the empty packaging.

Supporters say the expansion will boost recycling rates and reduce waste, bringing Croatia’s recycling system closer to broader European circular economy goals. However, manufacturers and retailers argue they are not yet ready for such a significant change.

Industry representatives warn that Croatia currently lacks sufficient facilities to recycle multilayer carton packaging and that most shops do not have reverse-vending machines capable of accepting Tetra Pak containers. Instead, retailers would have to collect them manually, raising concerns over hygiene, storage space and additional staffing requirements.

The business sector also expects higher operating costs. Producers of milk, dairy products and juices say adapting to the expanded scheme will require new investments, while retailers will face increased handling costs. Those expenses, they warn, could ultimately be reflected in higher consumer prices beyond the 10-cent refundable deposit itself.

Business groups, including the Croatian Employers’ Association, have called for the introduction of the new rules to be postponed until the necessary infrastructure is in place. They argue that expanding the system while businesses are also preparing for new EU packaging regulations places an additional burden on the sector.

The Ministry of Environmental Protection and Green Transition has acknowledged the request for a delay but says the industry has known about the planned changes since 2023, when the relevant regulations were adopted. Officials maintain there has been ample time to prepare and say they are working to ensure the expanded deposit return system begins operating as scheduled on 1 January 2027.

If implemented on time, the reform will mark the largest change to Croatia’s deposit return system to date, extending financial incentives for recycling well beyond traditional plastic bottles, glass bottles and cans.

World.title: Croatian Service Sector Grows, But One Industry Sees Sharp 12% Drop
World.content:
August the 1st, 2026 – The Croatian service sector has seen encouragingly strong growth, but one industry has seen a very sharp 12% drop.

The Croatian service sector continued its upward trend during May 2026, with overall activity rising significantly compared to a year earlier. However, the latest official figures also reveal stark contrasts between industries, as some sectors posted double-digit growth while others experienced notable declines.

Calendar-adjusted turnover across Croatia’s service industries increased by 5.8% year-on-year in May. Poslovni reports that when looking at the first five months of 2026, turnover was up 6.2% compared with the same period last year. Despite the strong annual performance, service activity edged down 0.3% compared to April.

The biggest annual winner was the film, video and television production sector, along with sound recording and music publishing, where turnover jumped 28.4%. Real estate activities followed with a 17.7% increase, while postal and courier services rose 16.2%.

Tourism-related businesses also recorded solid growth. Accommodation and food service activities climbed 11.2% year-on-year, with accommodation alone increasing 14%, while restaurants, cafés and other food and beverage businesses saw turnover rise 8.4%.

Compared with April, water transport recorded the strongest monthly increase, surging 14.4%. Postal and courier services were up 7.6%, while other professional, scientific and technical activities rose 7.1%. Accommodation services also posted a healthy monthly gain of 5.2%.

Not every sector shared in the growth. The steepest monthly decline was recorded in office administrative and support services, where turnover fell 11.7%. Air transport dropped 4.9%, while publishing activities slipped 3.3% compared with April.

On an annual basis, the weakest-performing sector was management consultancy, where turnover declined 9.8%. Office administrative and business support services were down 7.3%, while architectural and engineering services, together with technical testing and analysis, fell 6.2%.

Although May brought a slight month-on-month slowdown, the figures suggest Croatia’s service sector remains on a growth path overall, with performance increasingly varying between industries benefiting from strong demand and those facing more challenging market conditions.

World.title: Croatia–US Economic Relations: Tax Changes Open Doors for Diaspora Business
World.content:
July the 31st, 2026 – Croatia-US economic relations have seen a new chapter in the (apparently very long) book penned, opening doors for diaspora business.

These new and upcoming tax changes will open doors for businesses operating between the two countries, as well as for the Croatian diaspora who might need another more concrete reason to seek citizenship.

For very many decades, the relationship between Croatia and the United States has been built on more than diplomacy. It has been shaped by migration, family ties, investment, and the millions of people of Croatian heritage who have made the United States their home. Now, a brand new step in that relationship could reshape how Croats and Americans do business, invest, and maintain connections across the pond.

the old double taxation hurdle…

A long-awaited agreement on avoiding double taxation between Croatia and the United States is finally moving closer to implementation, bringing the possibility of greater financial certainty for individuals and companies operating between the two countries. Until relatively recently, this all seemed to move at a glacial pace, with many in both Croatia and the diaspora forgetting about much movement at all on the issue.

For Croatian citizens living abroad, especially the large Croatian-American community, the changes represent more than a technical tax issue. They are part of a broader trend: Croatia is becoming increasingly connected economically, legally, and professionally with its diaspora. For a great many descendants of Croatian emigrants, that renewed connection may raise an important question about whether or not now be the right moment to formally reconnect with Croatia and gain citizenship.

croatia and america, a story of immigration, migration and struggle

Ancient Croatia and the very new United States have a relationship that extends far beyond modern state diplomacy that we see all countries at least attempting to engage in in the modern day. From the waves of Croatian migration that took place back during the late 19th and early 20th centuries, to the creation of strong Croatian communities across major US cities such as Chicago, Cleveland, Pittsburgh, and New York, generations of Croatian-Americans maintained cultural and family links with their ancestral homeland.

During Croatia’s struggle for independence in the 1990s, the diaspora played a significant role in raising awareness of Croatia’s position internationally. Since Croatia gained independence back during the 1990s, relations with the United States have expanded into security cooperation, tourism, technology, investment, and trade. Looking at the situation as it is today, this relationship is entering a new economic phase, one where easier movement of capital, business opportunities, and legal certainty are becoming increasingly crucial.

Why this Tax Agreement Matters (in more ways than one)

Obviously, the primary goal of the Croatia–US income tax agreement is to reduce uncertainty for people and companies that have financial ties to both countries. Currently, individuals and businesses operating across borders often face complicated questions about where exactly any income actually be taxed, and how this problematic double taxation can be avoided.

They’re the basic questions. It becomes more complex as you delve deeper, with questions about what rules apply when investing, opening a company, receiving dividends, or earning income abroad often becoming too much for many. Understandably so.

The agreement aims to provide clearer rules and reduce situations where the same income could potentially be taxed twice. It includes measures related to withholding taxes, information exchange, dispute resolution, and mechanisms designed to create a more predictable environment for cross-border activity. A protocol signed in 2026 further addressed outstanding issues and is intended to support the treaty’s progress toward US Senate consideration.

For businesses, this could mean greater confidence when investing between Croatia and the United States. For individuals, especially those with connections to both countries, it could simplify financial decisions and encourage closer economic links.

A New Opportunity for americans with croatian ancestors who might want croatian and eu passports

The Croatian diaspora has always been one of Croatia’s greatest assets. Indeed, there are now more ethnic Croats born and living outside of Croatia than there are living in it. Millions of people around the world have Croatian roots, but many have never formally explored their legal connection to Croatia. There are a wide array of reasons for that. For descendants of Croatian emigrants, being granted Croatian (and as such EU) citizenship can represent more than a passport. It can be a practical bridge to easier access to life, work, and property ownership in Croatia and the European Union, much stronger connections with family heritage, new business and investment possibilities and the ability to participate more directly and concretely in Croatia’s future.

For many Americans with Croatian ancestry, the gap between loving dida’s war stories or enjoying Dalmatian gregada was comfortable, but there wasn’t enough of an urge there to try to get a Croatian passport. America is a country filled with people who value economic success and the grind in a way few in Europe do. For many, pursuing citizenship would need an extra push wrapped in a more economic bow.

As Croatia becomes more economically integrated with countries such as the United States, citizenship can become increasingly valuable for those who want to maintain a meaningful connection with their ancestral homeland, all while seeking business opportunities without getting ravelled up and ultimately strangled in red tape. Many members of the diaspora already visit Croatia every year. Some invest in properties, start businesses, or consider spending more time in the country. Formal citizenship can be the next step in turning a cultural connection into a legal and practical one, all without the threat of Croatia’s infamous bureaucracy on steroids.

From Tourism to Investment: Croatia’s Changing Image Abroad

For decades, Croatia’s global reputation was primarily connected to tourism. It would be a lie to say that is no longer the case, but things are altering. Now, the country is increasingly positioning itself as a place for investment, entrepreneurship, technology, and international cooperation. A more predictable tax environment with the United States could encourage additional economic activity, particularly among Croatian-Americans who already understand both markets. The massive Croatian diaspora has a unique advantage: many already have knowledge of American business culture while maintaining personal ties to Croatia. That combination can create opportunities in areas ranging from technology and renewable energy to tourism, manufacturing, real estate, and services.

What Comes Next and what does this all really mean?

In practical terms, the implementation of the Croatia–US tax agreement will depend on completion of the necessary procedures in both countries. There are still a few hurdles to jump, but the direction is clear and the track is getting shorter. Croatia and the United States are moving toward a closer economic relationship, and the Croatian diaspora is positioned at the centre of that connection.

For descendants of Croatian emigrants who have always felt connected to Croatia but never explored citizenship, this may be a moment worth genuinely considering. As Croatia strengthens its global economic position, those with Croatian heritage are increasingly asking not only where their ancestors came from and exploring their origins for emotional reasons, but what concrete, economic and business opportunities their Croatian identity can provide today.

croatianbydescent – turning heritage into opportunity

Croatian by Descent has helped many Americans pursue their interest in gaining Croatian citizenship, as it goes without saying that few know where to even begin. For the vast majority of the Croatian diaspora, the connection to Croatia has always existed through family traditions, language, memories, and annual visits to the coast and islands. However, as Croatia’s role in the European and global economy continues to grow, more descendants of Croatian emigrants are exploring what it means to make that connection official.

Obtaining Croatian citizenship is increasingly viewed not only as a way to preserve family heritage, but also as an opportunity to strengthen personal and professional ties with Croatia and the European Union. For those who qualify, citizenship can open the door to greater mobility, easier long-term stays, investment opportunities, and a deeper relationship with the country their ancestors once called home.

Navigating the Croatian citizenship process, however, can involve complex documentation, historical records, and legal requirements, especially for descendants whose families left Croatia generations ago. The attitude you’re likely to receive as you attempt to do all this is also a bit of a culture shock for many Americans used to smiles and client-facing service. This, is, let’s say… not so common in Croatia!

It’s precisely why many choose to work with the likes of Croatian by Descent, who understand both Croatian regulations and the unique challenges faced by applicants living abroad. They have noted an uptick in those seeking their services and help as more and more of the diaspora look to Croatia as more than just sunshine and sea in their ancestral village each summer. As Croatia and the United States enter a new era of economic cooperation, reconnecting with Croatia through actual citizenship may become an increasingly valuable step for a new generation of Croatian-Americans looking to turn their heritage into a permanent, unbreakable connection cemented with (another), stronger blue passport.

World.title: Svetac: The Remote Island Where History and Nature Meet
World.content:
July the 31st, 2026 – Svetac is a very remote Croatian island where abandoned history and wild, untamed nature come together in perfect harmony without any interference from humanity.

Hidden far out in the Adriatic Sea, just west of the far-flung island of Vis, the small island of Svetac is one of Croatia’s most isolated destinations. Also known as Sveti Andrija, the small offshore island is renowned for its dramatic cliffs, fascinating past, unique wildlife and complete and utter absence of permanent residents.

Located around 30 nautical miles from the mainland, Putni kofer writes that Svetac belongs to the Vis archipelago and lies just 2.5 kilometres from the volcanic islet of Brusnik. Throughout history it has been known by several names, including Sant’Andrea during Venetian rule and the local name Štondrija.

“a place for dreamers and madmen”

The island’s rugged coastline makes landing difficult. Towering cliffs surround much of the shore, leaving Slatina Bay on the southeastern side as the only practical place for boats to come ashore. Above the coast rises Kosa, the island’s highest peak at 316 metres, while strong sea currents and open waters add to its reputation as one of Croatia’s most challenging islands to reach. Croatian poet Tin Ujević famously described it as a place “for dreamers and madmen.”

Svetac also stands out for its climate. It is considered the warmest location in Croatia, with temperatures never falling below freezing. The island’s average annual temperature is around 17.4 degrees Celsius, comparable to Mediterranean locations such as Malta.

uninhabited since the year 2000…

Despite its isolation, Svetac has a long history of human settlement. Archaeological discoveries include ancient anchors, Roman remains and the ruins of a Byzantine fort. Benedictine monks lived on the island during the 15th and 16th centuries before ownership later passed to the Zanki family, who arrived from Italy’s Gargano Peninsula in the mid-18th century. The family originally settled there to harvest pine resin, leading many people to refer to Svetac as “the island of the Zankis.”

The island’s harsh environment has always made life difficult. There is no natural source of drinking water, strong winds frequently batter the coast and powerful southerly storms have claimed lives over the centuries. For generations, fishermen provided the islanders’ only connection to the outside world, sometimes becoming stranded themselves when rough seas prevented them from leaving. The final permanent resident died in January 2000, leaving the island uninhabited ever since.

wildlife and nature – svetac’s greatest treasures

Nature remains one of Svetac’s greatest treasures. Carob trees grow across the island, while it provides habitat for Eleonora’s falcon and Europe’s largest owl species. Mediterranean monk seals once frequented its shores, and the surrounding waters were historically rich in lobsters.

The island also carries a darker legend. Its pine forests were once heavily exploited for resin used in shipbuilding, while shepherds grazing church-owned sheep were said to have killed English shipwreck survivors. According to local tradition, this earned Svetac the nickname “Devil’s Island” among British sailors, reinforcing its reputation as a mysterious and forbidding place.

Today, although no one lives permanently on Svetac, its untouched landscapes, remarkable history and remote location continue to fascinate travellers looking to discover one of Croatia’s last truly wild islands.
