Following the video, Pirozhkova has periodically posted about the wave of online abuse directed at her. She has also publicly apologised several times, saying:

“I understand that many people saw it as disrespect towards the Armenian people. And I’m truly sorry. That was never my intention, and it still isn’t.”

At the same time, the blogger has acknowledged that she is using the controversy to promote her Instagram page.

“People recognise me now. Why shouldn’t I make use of something I’ve been through after putting in so much effort? I’ve worked hard for this. Why shouldn’t a person take advantage of circumstances and situations they have rightfully earned? I just want to change my life.“

Foreign nationals are required to respect Armenia’s national customs and traditions

The legal status of foreign nationals in Armenia is governed by the Law on Foreigners. Article 5 of the law states that foreigners in Armenia enjoy the same rights, freedoms and obligations as Armenian citizens. At the same time, it stipulates that “foreigners in the Republic of Armenia are obliged to respect the Constitution and laws of the Republic of Armenia, other legal acts, as well as national customs and traditions.”

The same article also provides that foreign nationals bear the same legal responsibility as Armenian citizens while in Armenia.

Armenia’s Criminal Code provides for penalties for “public statements aimed at inciting or promoting hatred, discrimination, intolerance or hostility against an individual or group of persons on the grounds of race, nationality or ethnicity, as well as the dissemination of materials or objects for that purpose.”

The available penalties include fines, community service, restriction of liberty and imprisonment.

Under Article 329, offences committed “through publicly displayed works, the mass media, or information and communication technologies” are punishable by one to four years’ imprisonment

Commentary

Political commentator Artyom Yerkanian said in an interview with a local television channel::

“After the Russian blogger publicly apologised, this story could have ended there. But some social media users continued calling on the Armenian law enforcement authorities to examine Nadezhda Pirozhkova’s actions and determine whether they amounted to a criminal offence. The authorities decided to respond to those calls.

Perhaps there was no need to be so severe. The court will, of course, take all mitigating circumstances into account.

Perhaps we should not politicise everything. It is obvious that the aim was not to incite ethnic hatred but simply to increase her audience through provocative videos.

In two weeks, the video attracted more than 250,000 views and over 5,000 comments. As a result, the number of followers on her page increased more than fifteen-fold.

In other words, this blogger simply found a ridiculous and foolish way to grow her audience.

Nevertheless, perhaps such cases should be monitored more closely, because this is not an isolated incident.

In recent weeks, there have been several similar cases in which foreign bloggers, particularly Russians, have made remarks discrediting Armenians and damaging Armenia’s reputation as a tourist destination.

There was one case in which a young woman accused an Armenian taxi driver of attempting to rape her. I also recall another similar incident, and there are probably many more. But what is more important?

Notably, these videos are deliberately amplified by non-existent users. An army of fake accounts is spreading this material in pursuit of a specific objective.

It cannot be ruled out that certain forces are behind these fake accounts and are interested in ensuring that Armenia is not perceived as a safe destination for tourists.

Every tourist who enjoys visiting the country indirectly becomes its ‘agent of influence’. Perhaps that is exactly what some people dislike.

I don’t know whether it is a coincidence, but it was precisely during those days that the Russian Foreign Ministry added Armenia to its list of countries where Russians cannot feel safe, citing the possibility that the Armenian authorities could extradite them to third countries. Perhaps it is a coincidence—or perhaps it is not.”

Social media reaction

“If, after a year and a half of living in Armenia, she still allows herself to speak like this, it cannot be dismissed as an accident or naivety.”

“The police should investigate her actions. She’s a planted agent.”

“She should be fined heavily and deported.”

“She should be tried and deported from our country. It’s a matter of the nation’s dignity.”

“If an Armenian had behaved like this in Russia, he would already have disappeared.”

“Foreign visitors are obliged to obey the law, respect the country and its people, and behave like guests.”

World.title: Meet Nitsa, Elvis and Oliver: Pine martens at Tbilisi Zoo. Video
World.content:
Nitsa, Elvis and Oliver are young pine martens and the newest residents of Tbilisi Zoo. A local resident found the orphaned cubs alone in an attic and took them home after discovering they had no mother.



However, pine martens are wild predators with powerful teeth and strong natural instincts. Once the cubs had grown up, releasing them back into the wild was no longer an option. Contact with humans had altered their natural behaviour, leaving them unable to survive on their own. Their rescuer therefore turned to Tbilisi Zoo for help.

Konstantin Pkhakadze, head of the zoo’s exotic animals department, said the pine martens arrived at Tbilisi Zoo about a month ago. He said such cases are quite common. People often assume that young animals found alone have been orphaned and need rescuing, but that is not always the case.

In most instances, the mother is nearby, hunting, searching for food or moving her young to a new location. Pkhakadze said intervening at that stage is the biggest mistake people can make. They should not even approach the cubs, as the mother may detect the scent of humans, see it as a threat and never return to her offspring.

Tbilisi Zoo currently has very limited capacity to take in new animals. Its existing site is overcrowded, while most of its resources are being directed towards the construction of a new zoo.

Nitsa, Elvis and Oliver were initially housed in the zoo’s exotics pavilion. However, the small enclosed space was unsuitable for such active and energetic animals. Zoo staff therefore built a temporary outdoor enclosure, giving the pine martens more space, fresh air and room to move freely.

Tbilisi Zoo‘s history spans nearly a century. It was founded on 10 February 1927 on the basis of the Caucasian Society for the Acclimatisation of Animals, which had been keeping wild animals since the early 20th century, though without official zoo status. The zoo was originally built on 70 hectares in the Vere River gorge. Over the years, the expansion of the capital — and later the devastating flood of 13 June 2015 — significantly reduced the territory of the old zoo. Today, it covers five hectares and is home to around 1,500 animals, each with its own story. In this video series, we will introduce you to the residents of Tbilisi Zoo. We will show how their day unfolds, how they interact with other animals and people, and how their behaviour changes depending on the weather and the season. Get ready to hear many fascinating stories.

Pine martens at Tbilisi Zoo

World.title: Georgia’s opposition launches campaign to restore voting rights for emigrants
World.content:
In Georgia, the opposition alliance Coalition for Change and the Strategy Aghmashenebeli party have launched the Emigrant’s Vote campaign, calling for the restoration of Georgian citizens’ right to vote from abroad in parliamentary and municipal elections.

Under the new Election Code, approved by the ruling Georgian Dream party on 17 December 2025, emigrants are no longer allowed to vote from abroad. Instead, they must travel to Georgia to cast their ballots.

One of Coalition for Change’s members, Tengo Tevzadze, announced the launch of the campaign, saying the initiative would culminate in a constitutional challenge seeking to restore emigrants’ right to take part in elections.

According to Tevzadze, the campaign aims to demonstrate that allowing emigrants to vote is consistent with Georgia’s constitution and that every Georgian citizen, regardless of where they live, should be able to take part in elections.

Tevzadze noted that Georgian Dream won just 13.4% of the overseas vote in the disputed 2024 parliamentary election, which the opposition says was rigged. He argued that this was why the authorities later moved to strip emigrants of their voting rights.

Tevzadze argues that depriving emigrants of the right to vote violates Georgia’s constitution and is unfair to a group of citizens that makes a significant contribution to the country’s economy.

The campaign’s organisers have set out two main demands: restoring emigrants’ right to vote and creating an electoral system that allows Georgian citizens living abroad to cast their ballots.

“We need as many emigrants as possible to sign the petition so that, alongside political efforts, we can also challenge the regime through legal means. Through a constitutional lawsuit, we will clearly demonstrate that emigrants’ participation in elections and their voting rights are protected by the constitution, and that Georgians, both at home and abroad, must be able to take part in free and fair elections,” Tengo Tevzadze said.

Voting rights for Georgian emigrants

World.title: Evening illuminations in South Ossetia: Video
World.content:
Evening illuminations in South Ossetia

Major reconstruction work has been completed in the South Ossetian capital, Tskhinval. The city centre has been renovated, dozens of streets repaired, and new utility networks installed.

The redevelopment of Theatre Square included new lighting, benches and marble planters, while boxwood and juniper shrubs were planted. Several school and college buildings, along with the Kosta Khetagurov State Drama Theatre, have also been restored.

The work was funded through Russia’s investment programme.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

Evening illuminations in South Ossetia

World.title: Russian mass strike on Ukraine leaves several dead and dozens injured. Video from Lviv
World.content:
Russian strike on Ukraine: Video from Lviv

Russia launched a mass overnight attack on Ukraine on 30 July, according to Ukrainian authorities, firing a total of 74 missiles and 284 attack drones. Ukraine said its air defences intercepted a significant number of the incoming targets, but some missiles and drones struck their intended targets.

Several regions across Ukraine came under attack, including Lviv, Kyiv and the Dnipropetrovsk region.

In Lviv, one resident was killed. In the village of Radushne, near Kryvyi Rih, a ballistic missile struck the home of a large family. Six people were killed, including three children, while several others were injured.

Lviv Mayor Andriy Sadovyi said the city had suffered direct Russian missile strikes on residential buildings for the first time in a long period.

The heaviest damage was reported on Paton and Vyhovskoho streets, where more than 20 residential buildings, a school, two kindergartens and other civilian infrastructure were damaged.

Rescue workers recovered the body of a man from beneath the rubble.

According to the latest official figures, 34 people, including three children, were injured in the attack on Lviv. Nine people were rescued from damaged buildings. Emergency crews are continuing search and rescue operations and clearing the debris.

Lviv city authorities said some residents whose homes were damaged would be provided with temporary accommodation, while municipal services are assisting those left homeless.

Russian strike on Ukraine: Video from Lviv

World.title: German broadcaster ARD investigates Georgia’s rise as a crypto hub
World.content:
Crypto mining in Georgia

“Crypto war: How Putin is using bitcoin to wage war against us” is the title of a 45-minute investigative documentary by German public broadcaster ARD, which portrays Georgia as a major cryptocurrency mining hub and an alleged transit route used by Russia to circumvent Western sanctions.

The documentary focuses on bitcoin mining and crypto systems which, the journalists argue, have enabled Russia to adapt to international financial restrictions.

Georgia’s favourable conditions for crypto industry

The investigation’s authors say Georgia has developed a particularly favourable legal and tax environment for the cryptocurrency industry over many years. They argue that this was closely linked to political and economic decisions taken during the rule of the Georgian Dream party and its founder, Bidzina Ivanishvili, turning the country into what they describe as one of the world’s cryptocurrency “grey zones”.

The documentary focuses in particular on the free industrial zones in Poti and Rustavi. According to the journalists, Russia can no longer sell natural gas to Europe at pre-sanctions levels, with some of that gas instead being used to generate low-cost electricity. The filmmakers argue that this electricity powers large-scale bitcoin mining infrastructure, the ultimate financial benefits of which serve Russia’s interests.

The German journalists say they travelled to Georgia and visited cryptocurrency mining facilities themselves, including infrastructure in the Rustavi Free Industrial Zone.

Russia said using cryptocurrency to circumvent sanctions

Nino Bakradze, founder of the investigative journalism organisation iFact, says in the documentary that Russia has not been completely cut off from the international financial system and is increasingly using cryptocurrency for cross-border transactions.

Nino Bakradze

She says iFact investigated exports of dual-use goods to Russia by conducting an undercover experiment. The organisation contacted a Russian trading company and asked whether it could ship around 30 drones to Russia. According to Bakradze, the company replied that such a shipment was possible and said it had carried out similar transactions before despite the risks posed by sanctions.

Bakradze says the investigation found that companies involved in such transactions use cryptocurrency to settle payments in order to circumvent sanctions, often without being detected by Western authorities.

‘Bitcoin mining in Georgia is profitable’

The documentary also features local bitcoin miner Nikoloz Museridze, who says the main advantage of mining bitcoin in Georgia is the country’s relatively low electricity prices.

Nikoloz Museridze

Museridze says his mining farm consumes about 2 megawatts of electricity. He estimates that, at this capacity, it takes about a year to mine one bitcoin, while the cost of producing a single bitcoin in Georgia is around $30,000-$40,000.

The miner describes bitcoin as “borderless money” that can be transferred anywhere in the world at any time and which, he claims, cannot be blocked or frozen.

World.title: Nauru withdraws recognition of occupied Abkhazia and South Ossetia
World.content:
The government of the Pacific island nation of Nauru says it has formally withdrawn its recognition of the self-proclaimed republics of Abkhazia and South Ossetia as independent states.

“The Government of the Republic of Nauru declares that it has withdrawn its recognition of the ‘Republic of South Ossetia’ and the ‘Republic of Abkhazia’ as independent states.

Accordingly, the Republic of Nauru has immediately terminated diplomatic relations with South Ossetia and Abkhazia,” the Nauru government said in a statement.

On 29 July, Nauru severed diplomatic relations with the Russian-occupied Georgian regions of Abkhazia and South Ossetia.

Georgia’s foreign ministry described the decision as a sign of respect for the principles of international law and said Tbilisi was ready to establish diplomatic relations with Nauru and strengthen bilateral cooperation on the basis of shared interests.

“The decision once again confirms that respect for and adherence to international law are the foundation of healthy international relations,” the ministry said in a statement.

The self-proclaimed Abkhaz foreign ministry claimed that Nauru had come under “unprecedented pressure” to end diplomatic relations with Abkhazia.

“The development of cooperation between the Republic of Abkhazia and the Republic of Nauru has consistently encountered resistance from Georgia and its Western partners. As joint initiatives turned into practice, a campaign of aggressive external pressure was unleashed against the Republic of Nauru.

For many years, states maintaining diplomatic relations with the Republic of Abkhazia have faced external pressure aimed at abandoning their independently determined foreign policy course. Small states, with limited resources to counter large-scale political, diplomatic, and economic instruments of influence, are particularly vulnerable to such pressure.

Such practice contradicts the fundamental principles of the UN Charter, including the principles of the sovereign equality of states and non-interference in their internal affairs.

The Republic of Abkhazia remains committed to strengthening its international subject status, protecting its national interests, and developing mutually beneficial cooperation with states that share the principles of sovereign equality, mutual respect, and international law,” the statement said.

Nauru recognised the independence of Abkhazia and Georgia’s Tskhinvali region (South Ossetia) in 2009, after Russia declared the two Georgian regions independent states. Nauru was one of only a handful of countries to support the move backed by Moscow.

Nauru is a small Pacific island state in the Micronesia region. It is one of the world’s smallest countries, both by land area and population. Covering about 21 sq km (8 sq miles), it is home to around 12,000-13,000 people.

World.title: Pashinyan: ‘Russia wants either exclusive ties or nothing’
World.content:
Pashinyan rejects exclusive ties with Russia

Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan has once again addressed the current state of relations between Armenia and Russia. He commented in particular on Russia’s restrictions on imports of Armenian goods, an issue that has caused growing concern in Armenia. During a briefing, Pashinyan said the country should view the situation not as a crisis but as an opportunity to diversify its economy.

Journalists asked him to address the political dimension of the issue, arguing that it clearly extends beyond economics. Pashinyan said the problem stems from Armenia’s search for alternatives that it previously did not have.

As an example, he pointed to the signing of strategic partnership agreements with China, the United States, the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, France and other countries.

According to Pashinyan, Armenia had never before had — and could not have had — strategic relations with so many partners.

“I cannot speak about Russia’s feelings. I can say that Russia sees this as a problem. There is also an element of exclusivity here. The issue is this: either the relationship is exclusive, or there should be no relationship at all. We do not share that view,” he said.

Pashinyan said Yerevan’s position is “legitimate.” Armenia’s ties with Russia are not exclusive, he said, but the relationship should continue.

“I ask that our position be treated with understanding and respect, especially since its legitimacy is not questioned in practice,” he said.

Pashinyan also stressed that Armenia would continue discussions with Russia over the economic restrictions that Russia and the Eurasian Economic Union have imposed on Armenian goods.

“That would be the worst possible course of action,” he added.

“What was wrong with Armenia? What did Armenia do?”

Journalists asked why Russia places such importance on Armenia’s political orientation and whether Pashinyan had given Moscow any reason to doubt that Armenia remains a reliable partner. In response, the prime minister posed a series of questions:

“What was wrong with Armenia in 2022 that the Collective Security Treaty Organization failed to fulfil its obligations? What did Armenia do wrong? Whom did Armenia harm? What did Armenia do that justified what happened?” he said, referring to Russia’s and the CSTO’s failure to respond after Azerbaijani forces entered Armenia’s internationally recognised territory in 2021–2022, despite the alliance’s obligation to act in the event of an attack on a member state’s territorial integrity.

What was wrong with Armenia that the Russian peacekeepers in Karabakh failed to fulfil their mission? Was the problem October 2022?” he continued, referring to the 6 October 2022 statement signed by Armenia and Azerbaijan in Prague, in which the two countries recognised each other’s territorial integrity. “But there were incidents even before that. What was wrong with Armenia? And why is it always assumed that we are the bad partner?”

“We are showing who needs Armenia”

Continuing on the issue, Pashinyan referred to Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko’s remark, “Who needs Armenia?”

“Has Armenia harmed anyone? Has it harmed Belarus? How can anyone speak about a sovereign state like that?” he said.

Pashinyan argued that the Belarusian president had asked the question but failed to find an answer. Now, he said, Armenia is showing exactly who values relations with it.

“Armenia matters to China, the United States, the European Union and Iran. And Armenia needs all of those partners as well. Georgia needs Armenia, and Armenia needs Georgia. Armenia matters to France, Germany, Poland and the United Kingdom. That’s the whole story.”

“The alternative is not yet in place” for a referendum

In recent months, Moscow has repeatedly urged Armenia to choose between the Eurasian Economic Union and the European Union. Russian officials have insisted that Armenia should hold a referendum on the issue as soon as possible. At the end of May, the leaders of four EAEU member states issued a joint statement calling for such a vote.

“I respect the fact that, on 29 May, the leaders of four EAEU countries issued a statement supporting the idea of a referendum on EU membership. But there is still nothing to vote on,” Pashinyan said.

He reiterated that it would make sense to hold a referendum only after Armenia obtains EU candidate status or once the issue formally appears on the agenda.

According to the prime minister, Moscow does not challenge Yerevan’s right to pursue alternatives. Instead, it is telling Armenia: “Decide today which alternative you choose.”

“But the alternative is not yet in place. The process of creating it has only just begun. It would be dishonest to ask people now whether they support an alternative that does not yet exist. They would ask many questions that we simply cannot answer today,” he said.

Pashinyan said the government would continue working to answer those questions before asking the public to make a choice.

Pashinyan rejects exclusive ties with Russia

World.title: Trump dusts off Red Scare playbook to stop 'mini-Mamdanis'
World.content:
US President Donald Trump and Republicans have been raising the alarm with voters about what they say is an impending political apocalypse for over a month.

Their dramatic warnings speak of a "dark road of death" and "a philosophical war to save" the United States itself.

The threat, according to them: communism.

Their argument goes like this: If Democrats regain control of both houses of congress in the November midterm elections, they will intentionally dismantle the country from the inside-out.

The solution was clear, Republican National Committee spokesperson Max Lippel told the ABC.

"It's common sense versus communism at the ballot box," he said.

" Republicans are on offence to ensure Americans know exactly what Democrats stand for and that their radical agenda is rejected in November. "

Republicans are unified in this message — and it's one voters will likely hear more of in the lead up to election day.

White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller said on Fox News last month: "Crazy communist lunatics … will steal everything you know and love in this nation, and they will never, ever let you have it back."

White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller told Fox News this month that democratic socialists wanted "to abolish our entire way of life". (ABC News)

Mr Trump has also made many attempts to warn the public, saying at a recent rally in Georgia that the threat is unprecedented.

"Including even World War I and World War II, Pearl Harbour, 9/11, I think it's the greatest threat that I've ever seen to our country," he said. "These people are stone cold, crazy."

And House Speaker Mike Johnson has gone as far as to say "communist" Democrats are a threat to voters' personal safety.

"I hoped and prayed it would never come to this, but here we are, the barbarians are in the gate … they are a danger to you and your family."

Socialism's US resurgence

The spike in anti-communist rhetoric has coincided with the growing popularity and influence of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), a progressive political organisation with chapters in all US states.

Politicians who are DSA members mostly run as Democrats, and even actively target establishment centrist Democrats to defeat in primary races.

High-profile members in public office include New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.

High-profile DSA politicians NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani and congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. (ABC News)

Democratic socialism is distinct from communism, although the true definition of both is often debated.

Both advocate for a society where people who sell their labour for money own the means of production, as opposed to owners making profit off of their work.

Communism is a more radical form of socialism that is often defined as abolishing the state and any private ownership entirely.

The DSA's policy platform is centred around creating "a world where no-one suffers … and everyone is free, equal, and cared for" through universal healthcare, affordable housing and stronger labour unions.

Bigger picture policies include ending voter suppression, removing corporate money from politics and abolishing the electoral college and senate.

In the past year candidates they've backed have stacked up dozens of Democratic primary wins across the local, state and federal level.

All those winners will be on the ballot as Democrats when election day rolls around in November.

Earlier this month Mr Johnson referred to them as "crazy little mini-Mamdanis popping up all around the country".

Three DSA candidates have won Democratic primary races for seats in congress this year. From left to right: Darializa Avila Chevalier (NY), Melat Kiros (Colorado) and Claire Valdez (NY). (ABC News)

DSA membership has surged in recent years, growing from about 6,500 in 2012 to surpassing 120,000 this year, the organisation says.

Polling indicates socialism is particularly popular with younger Americans.

A recent Cato Institute poll found Gen Z Americans had a more favourable view of socialism (53 per cent) than capitalism (45 per cent).

Republicans reanimate Red Scare

Part of the Trump administration's response to the DSA's recent success has been to reanimate the anti-Soviet and anti-Communist talking points of the Cold War-era Red Scare, said Clay Risen, a historian and New York Times journalist.

"It's the same story, it's the same basic playbook, it's the same back and forth about what is acceptable in America," he said.

The First Red Scare was influenced heavily by the Russian and German revolutions of 1917 and 1918, which both overthrew imperial monarchs and initially established socialist republics.

The growing workers' rights movement inside the United States also contributed to an atmosphere of paranoia about communism brewing at home.

Socialism and labour demands were intentionally made out to be one unified front by their opponents, often to crush the demands of workers, said author and communist historian Henry Prown.

"The collapse of the two into one often served more to slander labour activists as foreign radicals than to accurately describe co-affiliations," he said.

"Labour activists were persecuted as murderers, gangsters, and terrorists."

Mr Trump recently said communists wanted to blow up Mount Rushmore.

President Trump has reanimated the playbook from the Cold War-era Red Scare. (ABC News)

The second and more aggressive Red Scare came immediately after the end of World War II, with the start of the Cold War between the United States and the Soviet Union.

It was only intensified by the Chinese Communist Party taking power in 1949 following decades of civil war.

Mr Risen released a book last year about the history of anti-communism hysteria in the US during this era.

He said the legitimate hunt for soviet spies was regularly used as a justification to target tens of thousands of Americans with real or even perceived left-wing views.

"So for someone to be a communist had a literal meaning in America and an important meaning, but it was also weaponised and blown out of proportion," he said.

"If you use those terms and you demonise them, then it was easier to marginalise them, if not to criminalise the activities they were undertaking."

In the early 1950s, Senator Joe McCarthy used a series of hearings to accuse American journalists, public servants and military personnel of treason, for their supposed role as soviet spies.

Essentially all of McCarthy's evidence would prove entirely false, including fabricated documents and photos, but only after thousands of government workers were fired (~2,700) or quietly resigned (~12,000).

This period would come to be known as McCarthyism.

Americans were also targeted and blacklisted in the entertainment industry, as well as LGBTQ people, known as the Lavender Scare.

Special counsel on McCarthy's hearings was a young lawyer named Roy Cohn, who would later become the lawyer and mentor of a young Donald Trump.

Is Red Scare 3.0 a winning strategy?

Mr Risen said Republicans were using anti-communist talking points to portray policies many voters wanted as anti-American.

"A lot of people understand that large parts of the economy are broken, that our tax system is broken, that it definitely favours the wealthy," he said.

"And so people who come along and say, 'Let's fix that', that's very appealing to a lot of Americans."

House Speaker Mike Johnson said last month: "This is not a game, if they promise you free stuff, there is far more beneath those promises that even some of these people do not understand themselves."

Republican House Speaker Mike Johnson has warned "mini-Mamdanis" are spreading communism across the United States. (ABC News)

Speaking at a Christian faith conference on June 27, Mr Trump said "godless communists" would destroy religious freedoms and ultimately cause the destruction of the United States entirely.

"They will close your churches in this country, they go communist … they will kill your people, and that's what they're about, they want to end religion," he said.

"And as this spreads throughout the country, very much like an uncontrollable form of cancer, the country itself will be taken down."

In a statement, White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales told the ABC:

"The Democrats' embrace of socialism and communism is an existential threat to our country as these radicals proudly pledge to abolish prisons, private property, police, and even the presidency. President Trump will keep calling out their radicalism and draw a sharp contrast with his America First agenda. The choice between common sense and crazy has never been more clear."

Mr Risen said the Trump administration could get more aggressive as the midterms get closer.

"I wouldn't be surprised if Trump, because he has so much power … uses it to criminalise political movements, to criminalise political speech, to do a lot of the things that were done during the Red Scare," he said.

"There's a lot of legislation that's still on the books that gives the president and congress power to go after people who espouse communistic or radical ideas."

'Fruit of the same poisonous tree'

The DSA does not define its policy platform as communist, but Mr Risen said Republicans would still say they are to paint the entire Democratic Party as extremist and tap into many Americans' fear of soviet-era communism.

"[Trump is] trying to say, 'Well, socialist, democrat, socialist, communist, it's all the same'. In the past, that's been a very effective attack … a certain number of Americans are going to very quickly jump on his bandwagon."

President Trump said recently communists wanted to blow up Mount Rushmore. (ABC News)

A Republican operative told the ABC they are making these links because they genuinely see some DSA policies as communist. They said this recent Fox News interview with DSA co-chair Megan Romer, in which she supports having government control of large corporations, proves it.

Other reporting out of the US has suggested this link has also been a deliberate Republican strategy.

A memo prepared for the House Republican Conference by polling firm co/efficient, as recently reported by the Washington Examiner, advised its members to "do your best" to link socialism and Marxism to communism.

"Americans still hold communism as far more dangerous and alarming than socialism and Marxism," the memo read.

"So do not retreat to the softer label just because socialism alarms fewer in the abstract. Connect all three, fruit of the same poisonous tree, and let the family name carry the alarm."

World.title: French hitchhikers put faith in fellow travellers in Top End journey
World.content:
Ten hours waiting for a lift outside an outback Australian service station is not for everyone.

But for two young Frenchmen, it's their preferred way of travel.

Friends William Pertek and Manek Miquel have journeyed more than 5,000 kilometres from Queensland to Western Australia, largely by standing on roadsides holding cardboard signs in a bid to hitch a ride to their next destination.

The pair, who have landed in Broome in WA's far north, said resilience and faith in the kindness of strangers were key to their preferred mode of travel.

"You need to be resilient if you want to cross the desert by hitchhiking," Mr Pertek said.

William Pertek and Manek Miquel say the drivers they have encountered have been kind and generous. (ABC Kimberley: Esse Deves)

Hesitant to spend money on flights, bus tickets or hire cars, the 21-year-olds said they wanted to challenge themselves, improve their English and seek out adventure.

Mr Pertek said hitchhiking was not as common in Australia as in other countries, and was more difficult.

"At the beginning of our adventure, our friend told us, 'You will not do it, it's not possible,'" he said.

"We had the tricks … we cannot just keep our thumb up; we get cardboard, we write a town or petrol station on that and we just show it next to the road."

Free tent and sleeping bags

Carrying only a shared tent and belongings in a backpack, the men said hitchhiking allowed them to stop at memorable places, including small country towns.

They said Larrimah, a Northern Territory town at the centre of several true-crime documentaries and podcasts was one of their highlights, as well as Camooweal, near the Queensland–Northern Territory border.

Mr Pertek said Camooweal was one of the most difficult places to hitch a ride, with a population of about 230 people.

The pair says hitching a ride from Camooweal was difficult. (Supplied: William Pertek and Manek Miquel)

"This famous town, empty town — we [waited] 10 hours," he said.

But a free ride in the cab of a truck or passenger seat is far from stress-free.

Manek Pertek says resilience is the key to successful hitchhiking. (Supplied: William Pertek and Manek Miquel)

While they acknowledged they could not guarantee their safety, the pair said taking time to speak with potential drivers was imperative.

"[By] talking to lots of people before you get in the car, you feel safer," Mr Miquel said.

" You have to speak with everyone. If you never give up and try all day to find someone, you will find [a driver]. "

The friends said they were amazed by the generosity of strangers.

"Almost everyone [offered] food, drink, or help for something," Mr Pertek said.

One driver even bought them a new tent.

" He said, 'I can buy a new tent for you, I would be very worried to go into the desert without a tent to keep you dry … f****** crazy French adventurers.' "

Two women also gave the men $40 for new sleeping bags.

The friends were given a new tent by one of the drivers because their original was not waterproof. (Supplied: William Pertek and Manek Miquel)

'Tech-savvy hitchhikers'

Once more common across Australia, the crimes of killer Ivan Milat highlighted the risks faced by hitchhikers and sparked a decline in the practice.

But Fang Liu, a marketing expert from the University of Western Australia's Business School, said the practice was having a resurgence.

Dr Liu, who studies tourist experiences in Australia and how destinations are perceived, said a growing number of younger travellers were hitchhiking and promoting it on social media.

"If you're looking at 20 years ago, you may hear less on the hitchhiking in the travel space," she said.

"But because of social media in the last 10 years, I've heard a lot about hitchhiking."

The pair says drivers are usually eager to find out more about their hitchhiking journey. (Supplied: William Pertek and Manek Miquel)

Dr Liu said shared knowledge, improved internet reliability and phone tracking apps made hitchhiking appear safer.

"They will give tips, like the places where you can safely hitchhike," she said.

The mode of travel proved worrisome for Mr Pertek's mother back in France.

"My mum is very scared about that because I'm very young," Mr Pertek said.

" I share my position [location] with only one person … my mum. "

Meanwhile, Mr Miquel's parents saw it as an great opportunity.

"My father was almost jealous because he wanted to do the same thing," he said.

Different rules, different states

Hitchhiking is illegal in Queensland and Victoria, while other states and territories have different rules as to where pedestrians should stand and solicit a free ride.

Dr Liu said due to the increased number of people promoting hitchhiking online, more communication about the laws was needed.

"Check with the authorities or the police," she said.

"If an international tourist is coming from a country where hitchhiking is allowed, then they sort of assume other countries are okay with it."

John Hutchison says his advice to hitchhikers is simple: "just don't do it". (ABC Kimberley: Andrew Seabourne)

Kimberley Police Superintendent John Hutchison said he had noticed more people hitchhiking.

While it is legal in WA, he said his advice was "pretty simple".

"Don't do it," Superintendent Hutchison said.

"You don't know who the driver is, could be somebody who's quite a dangerous person, could be anybody that you get in that vehicle [with]."

World.title: Pet dogs trained to sniff out black truffle treasure worth $2,000 per kg
World.content:
A ragtag group of farm dogs and pets of different breeds and sizes are assembled in a paddock just outside Narooma on the New South Wales South Coast.

Their owners are nervous but excited about the prospect of testing their dogs' sniffing skills in a training class to see if they have what it takes to hunt for truffles.

Self-taught truffle hunter Kate Le Bars runs the classes, having spent the past seven years professionally locating the luxury fungus with her nine-year-old Australian Koolie, Hepburn.

"It's magical working with your dog and coming out to find the buried treasure," she said.

"On a beautiful day, it doesn't feel like work; it is just fun."

Kate Le Bars and her dog Hepburn work at the truffiere. (ABC News: Toby Hemmings)

With black truffles priced at about $2,000 per kilogram, turning the real thing into a training tool would be an expensive exercise, so a cotton ball dipped in a pungent synthetic truffle scent is used instead.

The lesson is simple enough: owners say the word truffle, then show their dog the cotton ball.

If the dog can then locate the cotton ball when the owner next says the magic word, they get a treat.

Ms Le Bars said as long as the dog had the right training, focus and responsiveness to rewards, any breed could pick up the skill.

"We had a Lagotto in one class, who were bred specifically to find truffles … and actually [a] little hairy white dog was the star," she said.

A mix of working dogs and lap dogs attend a truffle training class in Narooma. (ABC News: Toby Hemmings)

Truffle boom

Since their introduction to local soils less than 30 years ago, Australia has fast become the world's fourth-largest truffle producer.

Truffle hunting was traditionally performed by pigs, but as they would often eat the treasure after finding it, dogs and their 300 million olfactory receptors have emerged as more cost-effective sniffers.

Australian Koolie Hepburn can find up to 60 truffles in an hour of sniffing. (ABC News: Toby Hemmings)

If a dog does well in class, they are invited to the Gulaga Gold truffiere at Dignams Creek, south of Narooma.

"It usually takes one truffle season for them to be able to get to a stage where they're good enough, and then the next truffle season they become a professional truffle hunter," Gulaga Gold owner Fiona Kotvojs said.

Fiona Kotvojs owns the only commercial trufferie on the NSW South Coast. (ABC News: Toby Hemmings)

A successful truffle hunter will avoid distraction and sniff out the odour plume or "cone" that comes off the mycorrhizal fungus.

When they find the source, they place a delicate paw to indicate the location and not disturb the underground delicacy.

Black truffles can retail for about $2,000 per kilo. (ABC News: Toby Hemmings)

Up to 60 truffles can be sniffed out under the oak and hazelnut trees in an hour and marked with flags to be dug out later.

Australia is the fourth-largest producer of truffles globally, with commercial truffieres across the country. (ABC News: Toby Hemmings)

Sniffing success

The class has a mixed success rate, with only the cream of the crop making it out to the truffiere.

Some class attendees are there to learn skills for their own businesses, like Olivier Kapetanakos from Jindabyne, who has his own 2-hectare truffiere that is ready for its inaugural winter harvest.

He brought along his three-year-old cocker spaniel Ted, an energetic "failed medic dog", for his first day of truffle training.

Ted flunked out of being a medic dog, but his owners hope he will have more success finding truffles. (ABC News: Toby Hemmings)

"He's motivated by food, he's motivated by being with us," Mr Kapetanakos said.

"It's now just about channelling that enthusiasm to finding the truffle."

For others, the class is a fun way to test the teamwork between dog and owner, with the building blocks of the scent training able to be applied to anything.

"We had one person that was very keen to teach the dog to sniff out her wallet or her keys when she lost them," Ms Le Bars said.

"It's really good for the dogs. They love doing it.

" Anything the dog loves doing is worth encouraging in my experience. "

Kate Le Bars says teamwork between owner and dog is key. (ABC News: Toby Hemmings)

World.title: 'A miracle': World's largest gold bar made in Australia
World.content:
A gold bar produced in Western Australia weighing more than half a tonne has claimed the Guinness World Records title for the world's largest gold bar.

The Perth Mint created the 521.2 kilogram bar using Australian gold, refined to a 99.999 per cent purity.

Mint chief executive Paul Graham said the current world standard was 99.99 per cent.

"To get to five-nines gold, 99.999, not many can do that," he said.

More than 35 specialists were involved in the project. (ABC News: Mya Kordic)

" It's nothing short of a miracle. "

The achievement broke the previous world record of 300 kilograms, set by a mint in Dubai two years ago.

What's the point?

A team of more than 35 specialists were involved in the project, which Mr Graham labelled the "People's Bar".

Mr Graham said the idea for the project came a year ago, with the Mint conducting a "practice run" ahead of the bar's creation.

He said officials from the Guinness Book of World Records attended on site to watch every step of the process, which took up to three days.

Paul Graham says it's a "miracle" to produce such a big gold bar at 99.999 per cent purity. (ABC News: Mya Kordic)

As for what the record-breaking bar was worth, Mr Graham said he wished he knew.

"Naturally most people work out that the metal price alone is over $100 million, but something that unique, it's never been done before," he said.

As to the purpose, the bar serves as promotion of the Perth mint and its capabilities.

The Mint said the spectacle would help showcase the expertise of its local refiners and Australia's gold industry to the world.

It will eventually be on display at the Mint alongside another record-breaking creation, a one tonne gold coin unveiled in 2011.

Gold exports grow

Australia's gold export earnings are forecast to grow to $60 billion in 2025-26 from $47 billion in 2024-25, according to the Minerals Council of Australia (MCA).

Mr Graham says the gold bar's metal price is over $100 million. (ABC News: Mya Kordic)

That trajectory would see gold become Australia's second-largest export earner after iron ore, the MCA said.

The price of spot gold was about $US4,079 per ounce on Friday, according to the global financial data provider LSEG.

World.title: Why is a fertiliser company building Australia's newest oil refinery?
World.content:
Until this week, the name Perdaman was probably not front of mind for most Australians.

That changed on Tuesday when Prime Minister Anthony Albanese revealed the privately-owned multinational would lead plans for the country's first new oil refinery in more than 60 years.

The $4 million pre-feasibility study is set to examine what it would take to build such a facility along the West Australian coast.

Indian-owned but headquartered in Perth, Perdaman has interests in fertiliser, pharmaceuticals, property, chemicals, labour hire and renewable energy.

Oil refinery touted for WA The proposed facility would be built by Perdaman and be the first new large-scale oil refinery built in Australia since the 1960s.

Mr Albanese made the announcement at the company's Project Ceres site, a vast urea plant still under construction on the Burrup Peninsula, or Murujuga, about 1,540 kilometres north of WA's capital.

Much like oil, global urea supply chains have been thrown into disarray by the war in the Middle East, sending fertiliser prices soaring domestically.

Due to open next year, the plant is expected to produce 2.3 million tonnes of urea annually, making it one of the world's largest.

But for those living in the $6.4 billion flagship project's shadow, the emergence of Perdaman on the national stage comes with a complicated history.

Rock art removal

Murujuga is culturally significant to traditional owners and dotted with tens of thousands of Indigenous rock carvings, including the oldest known depiction of the human face.

Ngarluma woman and Murujuga custodian Samantha Walker protested against the Perdaman plant as it broke ground in 2023, citing concern for these ancient petroglyphs.

Ngarluma woman Samantha Walker has been a fierce local critic of Perdaman. (ABC Pilbara: Charlie Mclean)

Ms Walker said Australia should know about the company's dealings with Indigenous people.

"This is a company that has and continuously has no respect to engage … or consider anything that the traditional owners or the people of the country have to say," she said.

"If you can't listen to the people who belong to that landscape, who belong to the country and know the country best.

" They're just … skipping hurdles to get to where they want to be. "

The "hurdles" Ms Walker described related to the level of consultation between Perdaman and the five Aboriginal language groups responsible for Murujuga: the Yaburara, the Ngarluma, the Mardathoonera, the Wong-Goo-Tt-Oo, and the Yindjibarndi.

Murujuga's rock art is sacred and dates back 50,000 years. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

Three sacred sites were relocated to make way for Project Ceres, while another remains inaccessible at the outskirts of Perdaman's lay-down area.

They were moved with state and federal government approval after seeking advice from the Murujuga Aboriginal Corporation (MAC), which represents the language groups.

The decision was nevertheless opposed by multiple traditional owners and a letter viewed by the ABC suggested MAC had initially refused to give consent before later acquiescing.

Perdaman was not legally required to seek this permission as the land was already zoned for industrial use.

A map of Perdaman's Project Series taken from a report by WA's Environmental Protection Authority in 2021. (Supplied: Environmental Protection Authority)

MAC chairman and Wong-Goo-Tt-Oo representative Peter Hicks was present for the prime minister's press conference on Tuesday.

A lone demonstrator, Mardathoonera woman and Save our Songlines activist Raelene Cooper, was restrained by event security and ultimately issued a notice to move on by WA Police.

Raelene Cooper films out the front of Perdaman during Anthony Albanese's visit to Karratha. (ABC News: Kimberley Putland)

In a statement, Perdaman chair Vikas Rambal said the company had undertaken comprehensive consultation "as required under applicable Commonwealth and Western Australian regulatory frameworks".

"Throughout the development of Project Ceres, the company has engaged extensively and collaboratively with relevant traditional owner representative organisations," he said.

Mr Rambal declined to answer further questions from the ABC.

Push for Browse

The refinery pre-feasibility study pulls the fertiliser giant into another major environmental debate.

Last week in Federal Court, Federal Environment Minister Murray Watt defended granting Perdaman's neighbour Woodside his approval to keep operating its North West Shelf facilities until 2070.

He did so while acknowledging the resulting emissions could harm Murujuga's rock art, contrary to the energy company's own position.

Vikas Rambal pressed the PM on the ongoing assessment of Woodside's Browse Basin proposal. (ABC News: Alistair Bates)

The admission did not stop Mr Rambal from using Tuesday's announcement to lobby assembled politicians about another gas project touted by Woodside: the Browse Basin development, off the Kimberley coast.

"I don't know if the prime minister knows that the Browse project … has got lots of condensate," Mr Rambal said.

"We would request [the] prime minister, premier keep that in mind that all the condensate can go to this refinery project."

While Browse has mainly been spruiked as Australia's largest untapped reserve of natural gas, condensate may also be refined into petrol, diesel, and jet fuel.

Murujuga is already home to Woodside's North West Shelf, Yara's ammonia plant, and now Perdaman's urea manufacturer. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

Perdaman signed a 20-year offtake agreement with Woodside in 2023.

Mr Albanese flatly denied the study of a new WA refinery could apply pressure to Browse's independent environmental assessment.

"Processes are processes," he said.

Next steps unclear

Public records show Perdaman has donated $138,930 to the WA Labor Party since mid-2024, in addition to $11,500 to the WA Liberals and $3,000 to the state's Nationals Party.

Questions persist around the location of its prospective refinery and, Browse notwithstanding, where it would source the necessary oil.

Premier Roger Cook told reporters the focus would be on the state's Midwest and South West.

Roger Cook's WA Labor has received $138,930 in donations from Perdaman since mid-2024. (ABC News: Kimberley Putland)

But both he and the prime minister emphasised Perdaman was a safe choice for the job, having already received $475 million in government loans to deliver Project Ceres.

The company estimates the construction created 2,500 jobs, while 200 ongoing jobs will come from its operations.

"That's an investment that will produce a return," Mr Albanese said.

Addressing the news cameras, Mr Rambal added Perdaman had the skills to help make Australia self-reliant.

Analysts expect the refinery will cost about $15 billion.

World.title: Family pays tribute to Aboriginal man who died in police custody
World.content:
Family members of a young Aboriginal man who died in custody in Adelaide's CBD say they and their community have been overwhelmed by sorrow and grief.

WARNING: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander readers are warned that this story includes the name of an Indigenous person who has died.

Mourners last night gathered for a private vigil in tribute to the 23-year-old at Kingston Gardens on West Terrace, close to where the man died on Thursday, July 23.

The man, Kunmanara Ingkatji — whom the ABC has been given permission to name — was from Pukatja, also known as Ernabella, on South Australia's Aṉangu Pitjantjatjara Yankunytjatjara (APY) Lands.

Police last week said that he became unresponsive after resisting arrest and died at the scene, and that his death was now the subject of multiple investigations.

Among the 30-odd people who attended Friday night's vigil were extended family and Indigenous community members, including Jennifer Ingkatji and Nyunmiti Burton, who are older sisters of the man's mother.

Mourners took turns to light candles in memory of the 23-year-old man. (ABC News: Peta Doherty)

Ms Burton remembered her nephew as a "beautiful child", and said that when police told her of his death, she was so shocked "it nearly took my breath away".

"My spirit went down, deep inside," she said.

"I was just frozen. I was standing. I was just calling my sister's name. I was nearly [having a] heart attack.

"I gave the phone to Jennifer and the same thing happened to my sister."

Ms Ingkatji said she had been left grief-stricken, as had her community.

"They are still crying," she said.

"I was really shocked, you know. I nearly had a fit.

"After the police told us, me and my sister couldn't sleep 'til sunrise because we'd been crying, crying, crying."

Jennifer Ingkatji says she is grief-stricken. (ABC News: Guido Salazar)

Mourners were openly wailing as people took turns to light candles in memory of the 23-year-old man.

Some attendees wore bright yellow — the man's favourite colour — and held yellow flowers in their hands as they sang Presbyterian hymns in Pitjantjatjara.

The private vigil was organised by Pitjantjatjara woman Melissa Thompson, who is also an aunty of the man.

"He was loving and helpful and kind, and I'm going to miss his smiles and his laugh," she said of the 23-year-old.

Some attendees wore yellow, which was the man's favourite colour. (ABC News: Peta Doherty)

Ms Thompson said the man's death had "made us heartbroken".

"The community back in Ernabella, they are missing him so deeply. They have a sorrow camp and [are] thinking of us today, and they're the ones who gave us the permission [for this vigil].

"So we stand for them and the rest of the family.

"We are still grieving and we want to have the memorial here … and the loving ones to come together."

Melissa Thompson says members of the man's community "have a sorrow camp". (ABC News: Guido Salazar)

Ms Burton said the vigil had been good for the community.

"People are thinking about us from Northern Territory, South Australia, they are all thinking about us," she said.

Ms Burton says the vigil had been good for the community. (ABC News: Peta Doherty)

SA Police last week said the circumstances of the man's death were being examined by three separate investigations.

It said the Major Crime Investigation branch was preparing a report for the coroner.

A Police Commissioner's Inquiry and an investigation conducted by the Ethical and Professional Standards Branch, overseen by the Office of Public Integrity, are also underway.

World.title: Nina Kennedy is often superhuman, but in Glasgow she was a super human
World.content:
That's not how this was meant to go.

When Nina Kennedy steps into an athletics arena, the expectation is gold, and she carries herself accordingly.

The definition of a smiling assassin, Kennedy's friendly demeanour disguises a competitor's heart that beats with propulsive force.

It launches her down the runway and, usually, to great heights.

In Glasgow, Kennedy fell short of her own lofty goals and the standards we've come to expect from her, but still came away with silver in the women's pole vault final, albeit in a final that won't go down as one of the greats.

Kennedy snags silver, teen grabs surprise gold Flag bearer Nina Kennedy settles for silver in the pole vault and Australia's sprint stars return to the track after a host of medals at the velodrome.

Tailwinds at Scotstoun Stadium have been helping the sprinters, hindering the throwers, terrifying the hurdlers, and on Friday night, local time, making life difficult for the vaulters.

The crosswind kept the final from being a true jump-off between the strong field, with Kennedy clearing the bar only three times from seven attempts and 2016 Olympic bronze medallist Eliza McCartney winning on countback.

The top clearance of 4.65 metres by the gold and silver medallists was 30 centimetres lower than both of their personal bests.

Nina Kennedy came to Glasgow for gold. (Reuters: Isabel Infantes)

Kennedy topped by 1-centimetre McCartney's eight-year-old Oceania record of 4.94m just a couple of weeks before the Commonwealth Games began.

So, despite sporting a pretty gnarly scar from last year's hamstring surgery, there's no question Kennedy was fit and in form.

She carried her typical energy into the final, sitting out the early heights and waiting in the tall grass for her chance to pounce once half her competitors had already X'd out.

Why no other runner embraced the 200m gold medallist A doping scandal dating back to 2024 was the backdrop of the women's 200m final in Glasgow, and the frosty post-race scenes.

By the time she got out of her thick coat and stood at the top of the runway, piercing blue eyes fixed on her first attempt at 4.45m, half the eight-woman field was already gone.

She got over on her first go, but not with the sort of convincing clearance over the bar we were used to seeing.

Conserving energy? Shaking off the cold? No, as it turned out. Just a tricky competition.

New Zealander Olivia McTaggart stumbled at that hurdle three times, assuring Kennedy of a medal — and most likely silver at least after 2022 bronze medallist Imogen Ayris took three tries to clear 4.30m — but minor medals are not what Kennedy came here for.

Kennedy cleared 4.65m as her top vault. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

The 29-year-old has been in Glasgow as long as any of Australia's 255-strong team, having arrived early to carry the flag in the opening ceremony.

She has been so ever-present around the team that her success feels even more inevitable than usual, especially for folks who may have only watched her jump at Commonwealth Games, worlds and Olympics.

In those competitions, she had gone gold, gold, gold since her breakthrough win in Birmingham.

But so many things have to go right for an athlete to consistently catapult themselves 5 metres into the air with the accuracy and control required, and sometimes the pieces just don't quite fit.

Pole vault is hard enough in perfect conditions. (Getty Images: Michael Steele)

By the time she was preparing for her third attempt at 4.70m, the stare no longer looked so steely.

Having missed three of her last four jumps to that point, it didn't feel like a foregone conclusion that she'd pull it out in the clutch yet again, and so it proved.

"Of course I'm disappointed, I wanted to win, and I didn't," she said, emphasising that she was "genuinely really happy" to see veteran McCartney win her first major international gold.

"I'm superhuman most of the time, but I'm also human a lot of the time, and I make mistakes, and that's OK.

"I'm a high achiever, and I push myself to be that, but I think it's also important to remember I'm human and I make mistakes. I didn't want to make mistakes out there tonight, but I did, and that's OK."

The epitome of a big-moment performer, Kennedy has now not been able to defend her 2023 world or 2022 Commonwealth Games titles.

She missed the 2025 athletics world championships because of her torn hamstring and missed the mark in Glasgow, but results aren't all that matter for a woman who has ticked off every career goal at this point.

Kennedy was thrilled for Eliza McCartney (centre) to get her first major international gold medal. (Getty Images: Michael Steele)

She said before the opening ceremony that she would probably forget to soak in the moment as the team's flag-bearer, but after a long campaign and a surprisingly short time on centre stage, it seems she has figured it out.

"Sometimes sport is more than just the medals, it's about the memories made and the connections and the officials and the volunteers," she said.

"The crowd out there was so awesome. Everyone was just so happy to be here. I'm walking away with a lot of memories.

"I'm happy. Like, I'm sad, but I'm happy."

World.title: FIFA scraps World Cup sell-off plans after global backlash
World.content:
World football's governing body, FIFA, says it will not proceed with its proposal to sell a piece of its business empire to outside investors after the project was met with fierce resistance.

FIFA president Gianni Infantino said in a statement: "Having listened carefully to all the views, it has become clear that the project has created divisions of a nature that, regardless of the level of support, are no longer in the interest of the objective set out in the first place."

The plan was to raise $US4.2 billion ($5.9 billion) by selling about a 20 per cent stake in a new unit that would run FIFA events, including the World Cup, valuing it at $US20 billion.

The proposal, first announced on Tuesday, was strongly opposed by European football's governing body, UEFA, which threatened a boycott and accused FIFA of putting the sport's "soul" up for sale.

Gianni Infantino's proposal received pushback from all corners of the football world. (AP: Eduardo Verdugo, File)

The Confederation of North, Central America and Caribbean Association Football (CONCACAF) and the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) also said they opposed the plan.

Mr Infantino said in his statement: "[The] FIFA Forward Enterprise project was intended to provide a basis for further strengthening our FIFA Member Associations and our sport worldwide, especially in those countries where support is most needed.

"Our purpose has always been — and will always be — to unite and improve."

Senior FIFA advisor quits post A senior advisor to FIFA President Gianni Infantino resigned in protest at plans to sell a stake in the World Cup.

Earlier on Friday, local time, Mr Infantino's senior adviser, Carlos Cordeiro, announced his immediate resignation, calling the plan "a bad deal for football".

Mr Cordeiro, a former banker and ex-US Soccer Federation vice-president hand-picked to help grow world football for FIFA, said he could not "stand by while FIFA considers selling a stake in the World Cup".

"Let me be clear: I had no involvement in this proposal, and I oppose it unequivocally," he said in a statement.

FIFA's chief operating officer Kevin Lamour said staff were "deceived" by Mr Infantino, describing the proposal as a "project of one person".

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, meanwhile, told reporters on Friday that Mr Infantino was "the wrong man to lead the organisation".

ABC/Wires

World.title: Trump administration admits Reflecting Pool was a ‘botched job’ all along
World.content:
Updated WorldNorth AmericaTrump's White House Trump administration admits Reflecting Pool was a ‘botched job’ all along Michael Koziol Updated August 1, 2026 — 11:03am ,first published 10:02am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: The Trump administration has admitted that the damage to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool was the result of a botched installation by President Donald Trump’s contractor – not vandalism, as Trump and his team have repeatedly claimed. In a Friday afternoon court filing (US time), Trump’s handpicked federal prosecutor in Washington, Jeanine Pirro, moved to dismiss criminal charges against former Olympic athlete David Hearn, whom the administration wrongly accused of vandalising the memorial. The Reflecting Pool has now been drained. For the first time, the Trump administration admitted the damage was caused by a botched installation. AP Photo/Rahmat Gul Pirro said it was not until after Hearn was indicted that the Department of the Interior provided additional documents to her office “indicating that the damage … was the result of flawed installation by the contractor”, Atlantic Industrial Coatings. Also contributing to the damage was “the rush to complete the project prior to events associated with the America 250 celebration in the weeks surrounding Independence Day 2026”, Pirro said.



Atlantic Industrial Coatings received a no-bid government contract to renovate the pool and turn the water “American flag blue” after having worked on a swimming pool at Trump’s golf club in Virginia. It had not previously been awarded a federal contract. When the newly installed liner on the pool’s base began to peel off, Trump blamed it on vandalism. Without evidence, he accused left-wing vandals of cutting a 300-metre-long gash down the middle of the floor. Trump repeatedly blamed vandals for the damage without evidence, alleging they had cut the flooring with a box cutter. AP Photo/Allison Robbert But in court on Friday, Pirro admitted: “The damage was the result of a botched installation and not vandalism as initially represented by the Department of the Interior.” The new documents “significantly undermine the evidentiary basis for the indictment”, she added.



In the filing, Pirro says an expert inspected the Reflecting Pool on July 17, after it was drained for a second time, along with Pirro and senior employees from the district attorney’s office. They “immediately noted extensive damage throughout the now-drained pool” and requested all documents from DOI, which furnished them with 695 megabytes of additional records. Former Olympic canoeist David Hearn (centre) and his attorney Norman Eisen (left) after Hearn pleaded not guilty to the charges. AP Photo/Rod Lamkey “These documents indicated a rushed and flawed installation process, with repeated failures of the lining during the installation process, and extensive peeling of the lining throughout the Reflecting Pool. This was the first time that DOI made [the attorney’s office] aware of such information.” The filing makes clear that the installation was plagued by trouble from the start. As early as May 20, two weeks after work began, inspectors noticed “blistering in the finished portions of the lining” and alerted the contractor of the need for repairs, which occurred.



Work was completed on June 7, and a final inspection took place on June 9. But just two days later, a National Park Service engineer emailed both NPS and DOI personnel, alerting them to the fact that the pool’s lining was peeling off. He described the damage and included photographs. Pirro notes these concerns were relayed to the government “eight days before the defendant was arrested and the same day that fencing was removed from the site”, opening it to the public. President Donald Trump showing the media a render of the Reflecting Pool with its water coloured “American flag blue”. AP Photo/Alex Brandon A later report, following inspections by engineers after the pool was drained in July, mentioned various theories as to why the damage may have occurred. But over-spraying and a failure of the coatings to bond dominated their thinking, Pirro said. “Photographs from the report show the extent of damage to the pool caused by over-spraying and delamination. Damage was noted throughout the Reflecting Pool, and not just at the perimeter.”



Trump claimed vandals had cut a 350-foot slit from one end of the pool to the other. “I saw it,” he said on June 22, in the lead-up to Independence Day celebrations. “They cut it very violently.” NPS and DOI would provide evidence of the vandalism to the media, Trump said, but that never occurred. He also claimed six people had been arrested. National Guard members patrol the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool following reports of vandalism. AP Photo/Mark Schiefelbein On June 25, the White House issued a press release titled: “Radical Lunatics Deface America’s Reflecting Pool – and President Trump Was Right (Again).” “This isn’t random mischief - it’s targeted sabotage by anti-American crackpots who despise a strong, proud and beautiful country,” the White House claimed at the time.



The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the government’s admission it was wrong, or questions about whether Trump would apologise. Related Article Analysis

Trump's America The reflecting pool saga is a metaphor for the Trump presidency itself Hearn pleaded not guilty and maintained that he, as “a curious citizen”, only reached into the pool and touched a chunk of material that was already loose. On Friday, his lawyers said the case against him should never have been brought. “Its dismissal today does not erase the abuse of government power in arresting and charging a patriotic American who did nothing wrong,” the lawyers said. “The government’s approach was ready, fire, aim. The administration owes Mr Hearn an apology.” With AP Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: ‘Fill in the blank’: Why Australian sprint star had nothing to say about 200m gold medallist
World.content:
Glasgow: Australian sprint champion Torrie Lewis says she was told not to speak out about banned sprinter Adaejah Hodge, who won gold in the 200 metres at the Commonwealth Games but was only running in the race after her suspension for doping was discounted twice. Lewis came sixth on Saturday morning (AEST) behind Hodge, an athlete from the British Virgin Islands whose four-year ban was first reduced to two years, and then by a further seven months, by the Athletics Integrity Unit. Adaejah Hodge (centre) crossed the finish line ahead of Australia’s Torrie Lewis (left). Getty Images Hodge was originally banned after winning the 2024 world under-20 championships in Peru – a suspension that eventually meant Lewis was promoted from silver to gold. Watching Hodge be given permission to compete and win in Glasgow was galling for Lewis, who has previously said “anyone who has a drug charge against them will always have a taint to their name and some suspicion that come with that”.



The AIU announced Hodge’s reduced penalty in March. View post on X Asked about Hodge in Glasgow, Lewis said: “I’ve been told not to say anything of that. I would love to say some words, but not allowed to. “I think everyone knows what I would like to say, but yeah, just fill in the blank yourself.” Lewis won 100m bronze in an Australian record time earlier in the week. Getty Images



Lewis didn’t appear alone in her thoughts on Hodge. The other runners didn’t embrace her or shake her hand at the finish line. Hodge said she didn’t care what “haters” thought. “It [the last year] hasn’t been stressful. I put all that behind me. It is what it is,” she said after her win. “Things happen and I just wanted to move forward and see what I can do, work extra hard and show that I didn’t need it [performance-enhancing drugs]. I never will need it. I knew I had to put in extra work to prove to the haters that I am Adaejah Hodge. Hodge with her gold medal for the 200m. Getty Images



“It’s competition. Our goal out here is to win. I don’t really know what to say about that. It’s about competing. If you want to shake my hand, shake my hand. If you don’t, don’t. I’m gonna be a good sport and tell everybody good job.” Shaniqua Bascombe from Trinidad and Tobago, who won silver, said she didn’t pay attention to what other athletes did. Did she have faith Hodge was clean? “No comment. I don’t know what to say.” Loading



Hodge was initially given a four-year ban for taking a prohibited substance but had it reduced to two years when the AIU accepted her explanation that the doping was not intentional, and she had not deliberately administered the substance. Two other athletes from the Montverde Academy in Florida where Hodge trained also tested positive to the same drugs in a 12-month period, prompting an investigation and then charges against the head coach Gerald Phirri. Hodge’s drug ban was kept confidential by the AIU, against its regular policy, because it said making the ban public could have jeopardised an important ongoing investigation. She was given an additional seven-month discount, leaving her free to compete in Glasgow, because of her “substantial assistance” in an investigation. Despite the situation, Lewis was pleased with her sixth place. Related Article Commonwealth Games The strange rule that denied Australia a chance to race for a medal



“It wasn’t bad, you know. Considering this whole championships, I’m really proud that I made the final of this, and tried to put up a good fight,” she said. “If you would have told me at the start of this competition, would I be happy with sixth? I would have said absolutely. So I think after the 100 [final, where she won bronze] I just put my expectations even higher of myself, so I just still need to remind myself that you know, it was a big goal of mine to even make this final. So I’m still happy with that.” ‘Of course I’m disappointed’ It was a weird mixed feeling that Nina Kennedy could relate to. She won silver in the women’s pole vault but came away, disappointed – not only that she didn’t win gold, but more that she made mistakes and only jumped 4.65m. “I’m disappointed. Of course, I’m disappointed. I wanted to win, and I didn’t, and that’s OK,” she said.



She added: “I don’t think I’ve jumped that low (4.65m) in like four years, and I think that just demonstrates how tough it was. I know I’m in better shape than that.” In cold conditions, with gusty crosswinds, the world and Olympic champion struggled to find any rhythm. New Zealand’s Eliza McCartney, an Olympic bronze medallist who held the Oceania record of 4.94m until Kennedy broke it last month, beat the Australian on a countback, having not missed a height until 4.70. Kennedy missed at 4.65m. “You know, I’m superhuman most of the time, but I’m also human a lot of the time, and I make mistakes. “I’m a really good hot-weather jumper, but clearly I’m not a very good cold-weather jumper, and I’ll wear that.



“That amazing tailwind that the sprinters have been getting – that’s been like a complete crosswind for us. So it was so cold out there, but that’s a part of it. And Eliza did better. She handled the conditions better, and that’s why she’s walking away with gold.” Related Article Commonwealth Games Commonwealth Games as it happened: Gold for 19-year-old Aussie in the race walk, Australia sweep the podium in cycling ‘I gave it my best shot’ Sprinter Lachie Kennedy, who won silver and broke the national record in the 100m earlier in the week, had a similar night to Lewis, both showing perhaps the fatigue of racing day after day. Kennedy finished sixth in the men’s 200m final.



“Hey, I gave it my best shot but they gave it a crack. I came away injury-free. It was f--king cold out there,” he said. “I think we needed an Aussie in the final to show that we’re one of the best sprinting nations in the world. So I had to go out and represent. I probably didn’t perform as good as I would have liked, but I can’t be too upset, you know. I’m happy.” For Sarah Billings it took two world champions to beat her in the 800m. Billings won bronze just 0.03 seconds behind Kenya’s Lilian Odira, the reigning world champion. England’s Georgia Hunter-Bell, the world indoor champion who won silver outdoors at last year’s world championships behind Odira, took gold. That is the company Billings is now in, at the line with the two best women in the world. “I can’t believe it that I’m on the podium with them, and they’re just incredible athletes. And now I’ve just got to believe that I am too,” said Billings.
