World.title: Trump’s Gaza deal sparks questions on whether Israel, Hamas will comply
World.content:
WorldMiddle EastMiddle East at war Trump’s Gaza deal sparks questions on whether Israel, Hamas will comply Adam Rasgon August 1, 2026 — 9:58am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Tel Aviv: A day after President Donald Trump announced a new deal to begin disarming Hamas in the Gaza Strip, his Board of Peace released a 15-point plan on Friday, but key questions remain over whether Hamas and Israel will carry out the agreement. In its initial response, Hamas said that the “first step” would be for Israel to commit to ending attacks in Gaza and linked the turnover of what the group called “heavy weapons” to a list of other conditions. Trump arrives at Morristown Airport in New Jersey on Air Force One on Friday. AP Photo/Jacquelyn Martin The Israeli government has not issued a formal statement on Trump’s announcement. The text says the parties have two weeks to determine a schedule, which an international verification committee can extend. In underlining that Israel must first make concessions for the disarmament deal to move ahead, Hamas highlighted how challenging it will be to carry out the new agreement, which caught many by surprise when Trump announced it on Thursday (US time).



Experts and officials have raised doubts about whether Hamas and Israel will follow through on fulfilling the agreement. Questions remain, for instance, about whether Hamas will give up all its weapons and also whether Israel will cease its attacks, which is a precondition in the new agreement for further progress. View post on X The ceasefire agreement reached in October between Israel and Hamas required that the Israeli military end its attacks in Gaza. But since then, the military has carried out frequent airstrikes, which it said were targeting Hamas and Palestinian Islamic Jihad, the second-largest militant group in Gaza. In June, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Israel was killing all of those who had taken part in planning the October 2023 attack on southern Israel, as well as any elite Hamas fighters that Israeli security forces found. Nickolay Mladenov, the Board of Peace’s high representative for Gaza, wrote on social media that “implementation and verification have to be real”.



“Withdrawal must move in lock-step with decommissioning,” he wrote, referring to the withdrawal of Israeli troops from Gaza and the disarmament of Palestinian armed groups. Related Article Updated

Israeli-Palestinian conflict ‘Monumental step’: Hamas to disarm under deal for Gaza to get new government The Israeli prime minister’s office has yet to issue a statement on Trump’s announcement. On Friday evening, the government, citing an anonymous “diplomatic official”, said the Israeli military would not pull back from the “current yellow line” in Gaza without “genuine” disarmament by Hamas. Under the October ceasefire deal, Israeli troops retreated to a “yellow line”, leaving about half the territory still under occupation, but have since pressed deeper into Gaza. Itamar Ben-Gvir, the hard-line minister of national security, said the text of the agreement published by the Board of Peace was “unacceptable to Israel”. The targeted killings in Gaza “must continue”, he wrote on social media.



An Israeli soldier stands on a tank near the border with the Gaza Strip on Wednesday. Getty Images Trump’s enthusiastic announcement of the new agreement came days after he and Netanyahu met at the White House amid recent strains in their relationship. ‘It appears Hamas is kicking the ball to Israel.’ Shira Efron, chair of Israel policy, Rand Corp. Hamas’ weapons have been a key sticking point over months of talks in Egypt, one of the main mediating countries. The Board of Peace, the international organisation that has been negotiating with Hamas and Israel on Gaza’s future, has demanded that the group gradually give up all of its arsenal – a position that Israeli officials have contended Hamas will not accept. Armed struggle against Israel has long been central to Hamas’ ideology and a means to stay in power. Many members of the group view any deal in which they would give up their weapons as tantamount to surrender.



Trump signed the charter of the Board of Peace initiative at Davos in January. AP Photo/Markus Schreiber On Friday, Ghazi Hamad, a Hamas negotiator, said what was being discussed was Hamas “storing” its weapons “under the responsibility” of the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza, a committee of Palestinian technocrats working under the Board of Peace’s supervision. Hamas officials have said Israel must first fulfil its commitments under the October ceasefire agreement before anything happens to its weapons. The text of the agreement released by the Board of Peace calls for disarming Palestinian factions in Gaza after Israel carries out the commitments it made in the ceasefire deal it signed with Hamas in October 2025. In addition to the suspension of Israeli military operations, those commitments involve relocating Israel’s troops to an agreed-upon withdrawal line and allowing the entry of equipment to remove rubble, among other measures. Hardline security minister Itamar Ben-Gvir says there should be no let up in Israel’s targeted killings in Gaza. AP Photo/Ohad Zwigenberg



More than 1200 people have been killed in the territory since the ceasefire in October, according to the Gaza Health Ministry, which does not distinguish between combatants and civilians. The Israeli military has also continued to take over land in Gaza beyond the withdrawal line specified in the October agreement. In its statement on Friday, Hamas said the inclusion of “heavy weapons” in the agreement was linked to Israel withdrawing from Gaza, reconstruction, the establishment of a Palestinian state and other conditions. Related Article Opinion

Nuclear energy The US gave Iran its nuclear capabilities. Now Trump is giving them to Saudi Arabia Clinton Fernandes Academic and former intelligence officer The statement conspicuously mentioned only “heavy weapons”, while the text of the agreement released by the Board of Peace refers to Palestinian groups in Gaza giving up all their weapons. That text, however, makes an exception for personal arms registered with the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza. Many analysts have expressed scepticism that Israel will agree to withdraw from Gaza, especially ahead of national elections in October. Israeli officials have also rejected the establishment of a Palestinian state.



In agreeing to the disarmament plan, Hamas could be trying to put the onus on Israel to deliver concessions, analysts said. “For months, the narrative has been that Hamas doesn’t want to disarm,” said Shira Efron, chair of Israel policy at the Rand Corp, a US-based research institute. “Based on what we know so far, it appears Hamas is kicking the ball to Israel, knowing very well how difficult it will be for the Israeli government to execute this agreement, especially any type of withdrawal of its forces.” Ibrahim Madhoun, a Palestinian analyst close to Hamas, said that the militant group’s goal was to end the war but that it was concerned Israel would find a way to avoid carrying out the agreement. “Hamas did everything it could to deliver a deal based on reciprocity and simultaneous implementation,” he said. “Still, there are fears Israel could obstruct it.”



Efron said it was possible Israel and Hamas could soon return to “a familiar blame game”, accusing each other of failing to uphold the agreement announced by Trump while little change happens on the ground. This article originally appeared in The New York Times. Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: FIFA scraps World Cup sell-off plans, Infantino says
World.content:
Breaking SportSoccerFIFA World Cup FIFA scraps World Cup sell-off plans, Infantino says Updated August 1, 2026 — 9:51am ,first published 9:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

FIFA president Gianni Infantino said world soccer’s governing body has scrapped plans to sell a stake in the World Cup to private investors after widespread backlash. “Having listened carefully to all the views, it has become clear that the project has created divisions of a nature that, regardless of the level of support, are no longer in the interest of the objective set out in the first place,” Infantino said. FIFA President Gianni Infantino Getty Images Infantino’s confirmation came as one of his senior adviser’s quit in protest at plans to sell a stake in the World Cup as European football threatened a boycott and regional confederations united in opposition to the proposal. FIFA had proposed creating a $US 20-billion subsidiary, FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE), to run the World Cup and its other events, with a stake of up to 20 per cent to be offered to external investors. The senior adviser, Carlos Cordeiro, resigned with immediate effect, calling the plan “a bad deal for football”.



Cordeiro, who was appointed in 2021 by Infantino to help shape FIFA’s future, said the body was “mortgaging football’s future without any compelling justification. “It is a bad deal for FIFA’s Member Associations, a bad deal for football, and a bad deal for the long-term future of the game,” Cordeiro said. A former banker and ex-US Soccer Federation vice president, Cordeiro added that he had no involvement in the proposal and opposed it “unequivocally”. Meanwhile, FIFA’s chief operating officer Kevin Lamour said staff were “deceived” by Infantino, describing the proposal as a “project of one person”. “Our mission ... is to serve football. Not to serve the personal interests of a person who, unfortunately, believes he embodies FIFA when he is supposed to be at its service,” he wrote in a statement shared with the Associated Press.



FIFA had planned to proceed Despite opposition, Switzerland-based FIFA had previously said “incorrect media reports” this week had disrupted its planned consultation process but it would press on with the proposal to be considered by the 211 national football associations. Thrive Eternal, a fund run by Thrive Capital, founded by Joshua Kushner, was expected to lead the proposed investor group, FIFA said. Joshua is the brother of Jared Kushner, US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law. Trump, however, said he did not speak with Infantino about FIFA offering stakes to external investors despite having a close relationship after the US co-hosted the World Cup. British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who was critical of FIFA’s plan when it was announced earlier this week, told reporters on Friday that Infantino was “the wrong man to lead the organisation”.



Infantino, 56, is up for re-election next year and North American football chief Victor Montagliani is reportedly looking to challenge him. UEFA led opposition to FIFA plan European soccer’s governing body, UEFA, has led the opposition to the proposal, accusing FIFA of putting the sport’s “soul” up for sale. On Thursday, UEFA’s 55 member nations voted unanimously to boycott all FIFA tournaments, less than two weeks after Spain were crowned world champions. FIFA’s next major event is the women’s Under-20 World Cup in September. Hosts Poland said on Friday they had not received any information about the potential withdrawal of any team from the

tournament.



“Nobody is selling football. This is not something FIFA would ever entertain,” FIFA said in Friday’s statement. “Everyone has the right to express their opposition and to seek further clarification but no single entity can claim to represent all 211 MAs (member associations) around the world. “Each MA should be allowed to review the proposal and have a say in shaping their own future. These are the democratic principles of FIFA.” South American soccer governing body CONMEBOL said on Friday it had requested more information from FIFA on the proposal. “We recognise that the development of football requires commercial and financial decisions. However, such decisions must always serve football and never take precedence over its very

essence,” CONMEBOL said in a statement.



Related Article Analysis

FIFA World Cup FIFA’s offering Australia $45m to back selling the World Cup. Saying no might not be easy CONCACAF, the regional federation for North America, Central America and the Caribbean, rejected the proposal during a meeting on Thursday but the 41-member body did not follow UEFA with a boycott threat. The Asian Football Confederation, which has 47 members, issued a statement on Friday saying it “stands in solidarity” with UEFA and CONCACAF, but also stopped short of threatening a

boycott. The AFC, which has not historically been as frequent or vehement a critic of FIFA as its European counterpart UEFA, questioned the viability of the proposal and raised doubts about FIFA’s decision-making processes. Stuart Dykes, the director of European and Institutional Affairs at Football Supporters Europe, said such decisions could not be taken behind closed doors by a small group of people.



“The national associations should be demanding proper governance, proper consultation, proper stakeholder involvement,” Dykes told Reuters. “Football is not for sale. It’s a social good. Its value is created by the fans and the players ... That value is not for FIFA to extract in the interest of private investors.” FIFA says process is a democratic one Infantino said in a letter to all member associations that they would receive $40 million each if they agreed to FIFA’s proposal by September 19. On Friday, FIFA said it would not proceed with the plan without the support of the majority of its member associations.



“These principles underpin the FFE proposal: unprecedented development funding, truly global ownership of the commercial opportunities of our sport, and full self-determination through a democratic process for all MAs,” FIFA said. UEFA, CONCACAF and the AFC combined have 143 associations. However, not all individual member nations are certain to follow their federation’s line. The Czech FA’s President David Trunda told Sky Sports he could see the “positive impact of FIFA’s intentions”, but it has since rejected the proposal while endorsing UEFA’s stance. The Mexican Football Federation said it would study the proposal before deciding its position. Reuters

World.title: Before they find a new coach, the Waratahs need to find an identity
World.content:
SportRugby UnionSuper Rugby Opinion Before they find a new coach, the Waratahs need to find an identity Paul Cully Rugby columnist August 1, 2026 — 9:33am

August 1, 2026 — 9:33am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The last time the Waratahs were a rugby team with a crystal-clear sense of who they were was May 2014, far from the bright lights of Sydney. In New Plymouth, New Zealand, the Waratahs turned up and physically dominated the Dave Rennie-coached Chiefs. Israel Folau Getty Images They were too big, too strong, and filled with too many power athletes for the Chiefs to handle. They won the match 33-17. There and then, the Waratahs knew what they were about, and the rest of the competition got the message as well – they weren’t soft touches coming out of the Eastern Suburbs.



Twelve years later, does anyone have a clue what the Waratahs stand for? Can you describe Waratahs rugby in a sentence? Everyone knows what Brumbies rugby is. The Reds have a much more identifiable style after the Les Kiss years, and the Force are developing their own thing in Perth under Simon Cron: fighters, technically well-drilled, with a bit of a chip on their shoulder. Loading The Waratahs should have a rugby brand, given that NSW is an absolute goldmine for collision-sport athletes. There should be a constant stream of big men and superior athletes feeding into the Waratahs system. Everyone should know before the season starts that the Waratahs have the best raw materials to work with.



That doesn’t guarantee success every year, but it should mean that if all the tactical and cultural bases are covered off by good coaching, the Waratahs will be a consistently competitive side. They should be the Australian team that everyone loves to hate because of the volume and quality of players coming through. Instead, they’ve become the Australian team everyone loves to play. The 2026 season was another forgettable campaign for the Waratahs. Getty Images The failed answer to this problem has been to sack the coach, with Dan McKellar the latest out the door. As a result, the Waratahs have developed a saviour complex. It’s always the new coach who is going to save them.



But every time a new coach comes in, he brings new ideas, new thoughts on which players they need, and what style of rugby they will play. They’ve got it upside down. Those things should already be embedded in the organisation’s walls. The new coach should know exactly what he is stepping into the moment he starts, and that he is just a relatively small part of a bigger picture that started long before he was hired and will continue long after he leaves. Dan McKellar’s time in charge of the Waratahs didn’t yield great success. Getty Images That has not been happening at the Waratahs. Where is the consistency of approach between, say, a Daryl Gibson and a McKellar? They are chalk and cheese. And to emphasise the failure of the Waratahs as an organisation, they punted Rob Penney, and he then went on to win a Super Rugby title with the Crusaders. He was the same coach in Christchurch that he was in Sydney.



Calls to reinstate Michael Cheika, therefore, are surely rooted in the idea that Cheika is synonymous with the last time the Waratahs had a playing style that was theirs alone – lots of size, lots of natural talent and some smart guys pulling the tactical strings. Related Article Wallabies Kiss era is under way, but can he spark Wallabies in time for World Cup? I have no idea if a Cheika return would work. It is hard for the same coach to make the magic happen twice. But if it is not him, there will be enough men with enough knowledge and passion within the NSW rugby community to understand the 2014-era Waratahs blueprint and have a clear idea of how to bring it back. That could include 2014 Waratahs alumni Stephen Hoiles, now a young coach himself, but in all likelihood there will be plenty of parties whose blood runs blue who have roles to play.



This masthead reported last week that Rugby Australia was considering Joe Schmidt as an option, but he is not the right fit. In fact, the coach hunt isn’t even the Waratahs’ main problem – it’s the lack of continuity over the past decade. When you look at the Waratahs, with all the natural playing resources they enjoy in NSW, the first thought is: “All the gear, and no idea.” The second is: “What a damn shame.” They really stood for something in that short Cheika era. The 2014 title and the crowds that followed were simply a consequence of understanding who they were.

World.title: How the ‘Miracle in Mudgee’ inspired an unlikely bond between two Origin stars
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 How the ‘Miracle in Mudgee’ inspired an unlikely bond between two Origin stars Christian Nicolussi August 1, 2026 — 9:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

One of the first things Ethan Strange did when he was named to start in the halves for NSW on the eve of Origin I was to ask Nathan Cleary about the Miracle in Mudgee. Not to gloat about that length-of-the-field try that won the game in extra time – Strange wanted to discuss the other play he ran against Penrith that night. In the 75th minute of the Raiders’ epic 20-16 golden point win in round 25 of last season, Canberra were attacking Penrith’s line when Strange drifted from the left side of the field to the right. Halfback Jamal Fogarty threw a short ball for Strange on the runaround, and he used his speed and power to get on the outside of Scott Sorensen and inside Blaize Talagi to score a try. Cleary, a student of the game, knew exactly what Strange was talking about when the subject was raisedbefore Origin I. The chat came not long after it had become clear Strange would be starting ahead of the injured Mitchell Moses.



Cleary and Strange rehearsed it at the captain’s run on the Tuesday, then attempted the play approaching the hour mark at Accor Stadium as the Blues started their comeback against a 12-man Queensland. Strange, 21, playing in his first Origin game and growing in confidence with every minute, did much the same as he did that night in Mudgee – drifted to the right, called for the ball and steamrolled Cameron Munster to score. The play worked to perfection, but a mistimed run from back-rower Haumole Olakau’atu, who collided with Harry Grant while serving as a decoy runner, resulted in the four-pointer being overturned by the video referee. Four points might not have been the result in Origin, but the manner in which the playmakers replicated the move was there for all to see. The connection had been quickly established.



In the countdown to Saturday’s Penrith-Canberra clash in the town in NSW’s central western, Cleary praised Strange for backing himself on the big stage. “It’s a credit to him – it’s a play he likes, and as soon as he found out he was playing [Origin I], he came up to me and said, ‘Let’s run it’,” Cleary said. Origin halves Nathan Cleary and Ethan Strange will go head-to-head on Saturday. Getty Images “I was like, yeah sweet, and we got it on. Unfortunately, it didn’t end up a try, but it was nice to have someone there with that confidence to say, let’s do it. “All I remember from that night last year [in Mudgee] was me missing the field goal, then ‘Strangey’ cracking me with the left foot, then they ran the length. It was a pretty bad feeling. Hopefully we can turn it around on Saturday.”



NSW coach Laurie Daley recalled the pair discussing the play. “The only time I can remember them trying that play was at the captain’s run,” Daley said. “I knew once they got into the position they did in game one, then Strangey started to move, I knew it was coming. “You just wait to see what happens off the back of it. I thought it was great. You have to play to your strengths. “You don’t always see that play because a lot of the five-eighths aren’t runners – some just hold an edge – and you also need the power to do it. It also shows you what Nath is about and how he’s happy to listen and try anything – he’s all about the team. Related Article Exclusive

NRL 2026 Parramatta Eels rising star sidelined over safety concerns amid Sydney gangland war



“Those two will come up against each other on Saturday on the same side of the field. Penrith will know how strong Ethan is. He’s such a wonderful player.” The Raiders are chasing a fifth straight win in the hope of keeping their finals hopes alive, while Penrith are without Dylan Edwards (shoulder) and Talagi, who was dropped to reserve grade for Jack Cogger, and will do well not to let their attention drift to the next fortnight when top-four opponents the Warriors and Sydney Roosters await.

World.title: Trump administration admits Reflecting Pool was a ‘botched job’ all along
World.content:
Updated WorldNorth AmericaTrump's White House Trump administration admits Reflecting Pool was a ‘botched job’ all along Michael Koziol Updated August 1, 2026 — 11:03am ,first published 10:02am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: The Trump administration has admitted that the damage to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool was the result of a botched installation by President Donald Trump’s contractor – not vandalism, as Trump and his team have repeatedly claimed. In a Friday afternoon court filing (US time), Trump’s handpicked federal prosecutor in Washington, Jeanine Pirro, moved to dismiss criminal charges against former Olympic athlete David Hearn, whom the administration wrongly accused of vandalising the memorial. The Reflecting Pool has now been drained. For the first time, the Trump administration admitted the damage was caused by a botched installation. AP Photo/Rahmat Gul Pirro said it was not until after Hearn was indicted that the Department of the Interior provided additional documents to her office “indicating that the damage … was the result of flawed installation by the contractor”, Atlantic Industrial Coatings. Also contributing to the damage was “the rush to complete the project prior to events associated with the America 250 celebration in the weeks surrounding Independence Day 2026”, Pirro said.



Atlantic Industrial Coatings received a no-bid government contract to renovate the pool and turn the water “American flag blue” after having worked on a swimming pool at Trump’s golf club in Virginia. It had not previously been awarded a federal contract. When the newly installed liner on the pool’s base began to peel off, Trump blamed it on vandalism. Without evidence, he accused left-wing vandals of cutting a 300-metre-long gash down the middle of the floor. Trump repeatedly blamed vandals for the damage without evidence, alleging they had cut the flooring with a box cutter. AP Photo/Allison Robbert But in court on Friday, Pirro admitted: “The damage was the result of a botched installation and not vandalism as initially represented by the Department of the Interior.” The new documents “significantly undermine the evidentiary basis for the indictment”, she added.



In the filing, Pirro says an expert inspected the Reflecting Pool on July 17, after it was drained for a second time, along with Pirro and senior employees from the district attorney’s office. They “immediately noted extensive damage throughout the now-drained pool” and requested all documents from DOI, which furnished them with 695 megabytes of additional records. Former Olympic canoeist David Hearn (centre) and his attorney Norman Eisen (left) after Hearn pleaded not guilty to the charges. AP Photo/Rod Lamkey “These documents indicated a rushed and flawed installation process, with repeated failures of the lining during the installation process, and extensive peeling of the lining throughout the Reflecting Pool. This was the first time that DOI made [the attorney’s office] aware of such information.” The filing makes clear that the installation was plagued by trouble from the start. As early as May 20, two weeks after work began, inspectors noticed “blistering in the finished portions of the lining” and alerted the contractor of the need for repairs, which occurred.



Work was completed on June 7, and a final inspection took place on June 9. But just two days later, a National Park Service engineer emailed both NPS and DOI personnel, alerting them to the fact that the pool’s lining was peeling off. He described the damage and included photographs. Pirro notes these concerns were relayed to the government “eight days before the defendant was arrested and the same day that fencing was removed from the site”, opening it to the public. President Donald Trump showing the media a render of the Reflecting Pool with its water coloured “American flag blue”. AP Photo/Alex Brandon A later report, following inspections by engineers after the pool was drained in July, mentioned various theories as to why the damage may have occurred. But over-spraying and a failure of the coatings to bond dominated their thinking, Pirro said. “Photographs from the report show the extent of damage to the pool caused by over-spraying and delamination. Damage was noted throughout the Reflecting Pool, and not just at the perimeter.”



Trump claimed vandals had cut a 350-foot slit from one end of the pool to the other. “I saw it,” he said on June 22, in the lead-up to Independence Day celebrations. “They cut it very violently.” NPS and DOI would provide evidence of the vandalism to the media, Trump said, but that never occurred. He also claimed six people had been arrested. National Guard members patrol the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool following reports of vandalism. AP Photo/Mark Schiefelbein On June 25, the White House issued a press release titled: “Radical Lunatics Deface America’s Reflecting Pool – and President Trump Was Right (Again).” “This isn’t random mischief - it’s targeted sabotage by anti-American crackpots who despise a strong, proud and beautiful country,” the White House claimed at the time.



The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the government’s admission it was wrong, or questions about whether Trump would apologise. Related Article Analysis

Trump's America The reflecting pool saga is a metaphor for the Trump presidency itself Hearn pleaded not guilty and maintained that he, as “a curious citizen”, only reached into the pool and touched a chunk of material that was already loose. On Friday, his lawyers said the case against him should never have been brought. “Its dismissal today does not erase the abuse of government power in arresting and charging a patriotic American who did nothing wrong,” the lawyers said. “The government’s approach was ready, fire, aim. The administration owes Mr Hearn an apology.” With AP Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: ‘Fill in the blank’: Why Australian sprint star had nothing to say about 200m gold medallist
World.content:
Glasgow: Australian sprint champion Torrie Lewis says she was told not to speak out about banned sprinter Adaejah Hodge, who won gold in the 200 metres at the Commonwealth Games but was only running in the race after her suspension for doping was discounted twice. Lewis came sixth on Saturday morning (AEST) behind Hodge, an athlete from the British Virgin Islands whose four-year ban was first reduced to two years, and then by a further seven months, by the Athletics Integrity Unit. Adaejah Hodge (centre) crossed the finish line ahead of Australia’s Torrie Lewis (left). Getty Images Hodge was originally banned after winning the 2024 world under-20 championships in Peru – a suspension that eventually meant Lewis was promoted from silver to gold. Watching Hodge be given permission to compete and win in Glasgow was galling for Lewis, who has previously said “anyone who has a drug charge against them will always have a taint to their name and some suspicion that come with that”.



The AIU announced Hodge’s reduced penalty in March. View post on X Asked about Hodge in Glasgow, Lewis said: “I’ve been told not to say anything of that. I would love to say some words, but not allowed to. “I think everyone knows what I would like to say, but yeah, just fill in the blank yourself.” Lewis won 100m bronze in an Australian record time earlier in the week. Getty Images



Lewis didn’t appear alone in her thoughts on Hodge. The other runners didn’t embrace her or shake her hand at the finish line. Hodge said she didn’t care what “haters” thought. “It [the last year] hasn’t been stressful. I put all that behind me. It is what it is,” she said after her win. “Things happen and I just wanted to move forward and see what I can do, work extra hard and show that I didn’t need it [performance-enhancing drugs]. I never will need it. I knew I had to put in extra work to prove to the haters that I am Adaejah Hodge. Hodge with her gold medal for the 200m. Getty Images



“It’s competition. Our goal out here is to win. I don’t really know what to say about that. It’s about competing. If you want to shake my hand, shake my hand. If you don’t, don’t. I’m gonna be a good sport and tell everybody good job.” Shaniqua Bascombe from Trinidad and Tobago, who won silver, said she didn’t pay attention to what other athletes did. Did she have faith Hodge was clean? “No comment. I don’t know what to say.” Loading



Hodge was initially given a four-year ban for taking a prohibited substance but had it reduced to two years when the AIU accepted her explanation that the doping was not intentional, and she had not deliberately administered the substance. Two other athletes from the Montverde Academy in Florida where Hodge trained also tested positive to the same drugs in a 12-month period, prompting an investigation and then charges against the head coach Gerald Phirri. Hodge’s drug ban was kept confidential by the AIU, against its regular policy, because it said making the ban public could have jeopardised an important ongoing investigation. She was given an additional seven-month discount, leaving her free to compete in Glasgow, because of her “substantial assistance” in an investigation. Despite the situation, Lewis was pleased with her sixth place. Related Article Commonwealth Games The strange rule that denied Australia a chance to race for a medal



“It wasn’t bad, you know. Considering this whole championships, I’m really proud that I made the final of this, and tried to put up a good fight,” she said. “If you would have told me at the start of this competition, would I be happy with sixth? I would have said absolutely. So I think after the 100 [final, where she won bronze] I just put my expectations even higher of myself, so I just still need to remind myself that you know, it was a big goal of mine to even make this final. So I’m still happy with that.” ‘Of course I’m disappointed’ It was a weird mixed feeling that Nina Kennedy could relate to. She won silver in the women’s pole vault but came away, disappointed – not only that she didn’t win gold, but more that she made mistakes and only jumped 4.65m. “I’m disappointed. Of course, I’m disappointed. I wanted to win, and I didn’t, and that’s OK,” she said.



She added: “I don’t think I’ve jumped that low (4.65m) in like four years, and I think that just demonstrates how tough it was. I know I’m in better shape than that.” In cold conditions, with gusty crosswinds, the world and Olympic champion struggled to find any rhythm. New Zealand’s Eliza McCartney, an Olympic bronze medallist who held the Oceania record of 4.94m until Kennedy broke it last month, beat the Australian on a countback, having not missed a height until 4.70. Kennedy missed at 4.65m. “You know, I’m superhuman most of the time, but I’m also human a lot of the time, and I make mistakes. “I’m a really good hot-weather jumper, but clearly I’m not a very good cold-weather jumper, and I’ll wear that.



“That amazing tailwind that the sprinters have been getting – that’s been like a complete crosswind for us. So it was so cold out there, but that’s a part of it. And Eliza did better. She handled the conditions better, and that’s why she’s walking away with gold.” Related Article Commonwealth Games Commonwealth Games as it happened: Gold for 19-year-old Aussie in the race walk, Australia sweep the podium in cycling ‘I gave it my best shot’ Sprinter Lachie Kennedy, who won silver and broke the national record in the 100m earlier in the week, had a similar night to Lewis, both showing perhaps the fatigue of racing day after day. Kennedy finished sixth in the men’s 200m final.



“Hey, I gave it my best shot but they gave it a crack. I came away injury-free. It was f--king cold out there,” he said. “I think we needed an Aussie in the final to show that we’re one of the best sprinting nations in the world. So I had to go out and represent. I probably didn’t perform as good as I would have liked, but I can’t be too upset, you know. I’m happy.” For Sarah Billings it took two world champions to beat her in the 800m. Billings won bronze just 0.03 seconds behind Kenya’s Lilian Odira, the reigning world champion. England’s Georgia Hunter-Bell, the world indoor champion who won silver outdoors at last year’s world championships behind Odira, took gold. That is the company Billings is now in, at the line with the two best women in the world. “I can’t believe it that I’m on the podium with them, and they’re just incredible athletes. And now I’ve just got to believe that I am too,” said Billings.

World.title: Trump’s Gaza deal sparks questions on whether Israel, Hamas will comply
World.content:
WorldMiddle EastMiddle East at war Trump’s Gaza deal sparks questions on whether Israel, Hamas will comply Adam Rasgon August 1, 2026 — 9:58am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Tel Aviv: A day after President Donald Trump announced a new deal to begin disarming Hamas in the Gaza Strip, his Board of Peace released a 15-point plan on Friday, but key questions remain over whether Hamas and Israel will carry out the agreement. In its initial response, Hamas said that the “first step” would be for Israel to commit to ending attacks in Gaza and linked the turnover of what the group called “heavy weapons” to a list of other conditions. Trump arrives at Morristown Airport in New Jersey on Air Force One on Friday. AP Photo/Jacquelyn Martin The Israeli government has not issued a formal statement on Trump’s announcement. The text says the parties have two weeks to determine a schedule, which an international verification committee can extend. In underlining that Israel must first make concessions for the disarmament deal to move ahead, Hamas highlighted how challenging it will be to carry out the new agreement, which caught many by surprise when Trump announced it on Thursday (US time).



Experts and officials have raised doubts about whether Hamas and Israel will follow through on fulfilling the agreement. Questions remain, for instance, about whether Hamas will give up all its weapons and also whether Israel will cease its attacks, which is a precondition in the new agreement for further progress. View post on X The ceasefire agreement reached in October between Israel and Hamas required that the Israeli military end its attacks in Gaza. But since then, the military has carried out frequent airstrikes, which it said were targeting Hamas and Palestinian Islamic Jihad, the second-largest militant group in Gaza. In June, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Israel was killing all of those who had taken part in planning the October 2023 attack on southern Israel, as well as any elite Hamas fighters that Israeli security forces found. Nickolay Mladenov, the Board of Peace’s high representative for Gaza, wrote on social media that “implementation and verification have to be real”.



“Withdrawal must move in lock-step with decommissioning,” he wrote, referring to the withdrawal of Israeli troops from Gaza and the disarmament of Palestinian armed groups. Related Article Updated

Israeli-Palestinian conflict ‘Monumental step’: Hamas to disarm under deal for Gaza to get new government The Israeli prime minister’s office has yet to issue a statement on Trump’s announcement. On Friday evening, the government, citing an anonymous “diplomatic official”, said the Israeli military would not pull back from the “current yellow line” in Gaza without “genuine” disarmament by Hamas. Under the October ceasefire deal, Israeli troops retreated to a “yellow line”, leaving about half the territory still under occupation, but have since pressed deeper into Gaza. Itamar Ben-Gvir, the hard-line minister of national security, said the text of the agreement published by the Board of Peace was “unacceptable to Israel”. The targeted killings in Gaza “must continue”, he wrote on social media.



An Israeli soldier stands on a tank near the border with the Gaza Strip on Wednesday. Getty Images Trump’s enthusiastic announcement of the new agreement came days after he and Netanyahu met at the White House amid recent strains in their relationship. ‘It appears Hamas is kicking the ball to Israel.’ Shira Efron, chair of Israel policy, Rand Corp. Hamas’ weapons have been a key sticking point over months of talks in Egypt, one of the main mediating countries. The Board of Peace, the international organisation that has been negotiating with Hamas and Israel on Gaza’s future, has demanded that the group gradually give up all of its arsenal – a position that Israeli officials have contended Hamas will not accept. Armed struggle against Israel has long been central to Hamas’ ideology and a means to stay in power. Many members of the group view any deal in which they would give up their weapons as tantamount to surrender.



Trump signed the charter of the Board of Peace initiative at Davos in January. AP Photo/Markus Schreiber On Friday, Ghazi Hamad, a Hamas negotiator, said what was being discussed was Hamas “storing” its weapons “under the responsibility” of the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza, a committee of Palestinian technocrats working under the Board of Peace’s supervision. Hamas officials have said Israel must first fulfil its commitments under the October ceasefire agreement before anything happens to its weapons. The text of the agreement released by the Board of Peace calls for disarming Palestinian factions in Gaza after Israel carries out the commitments it made in the ceasefire deal it signed with Hamas in October 2025. In addition to the suspension of Israeli military operations, those commitments involve relocating Israel’s troops to an agreed-upon withdrawal line and allowing the entry of equipment to remove rubble, among other measures. Hardline security minister Itamar Ben-Gvir says there should be no let up in Israel’s targeted killings in Gaza. AP Photo/Ohad Zwigenberg



More than 1200 people have been killed in the territory since the ceasefire in October, according to the Gaza Health Ministry, which does not distinguish between combatants and civilians. The Israeli military has also continued to take over land in Gaza beyond the withdrawal line specified in the October agreement. In its statement on Friday, Hamas said the inclusion of “heavy weapons” in the agreement was linked to Israel withdrawing from Gaza, reconstruction, the establishment of a Palestinian state and other conditions. Related Article Opinion

Nuclear energy The US gave Iran its nuclear capabilities. Now Trump is giving them to Saudi Arabia Clinton Fernandes Academic and former intelligence officer The statement conspicuously mentioned only “heavy weapons”, while the text of the agreement released by the Board of Peace refers to Palestinian groups in Gaza giving up all their weapons. That text, however, makes an exception for personal arms registered with the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza. Many analysts have expressed scepticism that Israel will agree to withdraw from Gaza, especially ahead of national elections in October. Israeli officials have also rejected the establishment of a Palestinian state.



In agreeing to the disarmament plan, Hamas could be trying to put the onus on Israel to deliver concessions, analysts said. “For months, the narrative has been that Hamas doesn’t want to disarm,” said Shira Efron, chair of Israel policy at the Rand Corp, a US-based research institute. “Based on what we know so far, it appears Hamas is kicking the ball to Israel, knowing very well how difficult it will be for the Israeli government to execute this agreement, especially any type of withdrawal of its forces.” Ibrahim Madhoun, a Palestinian analyst close to Hamas, said that the militant group’s goal was to end the war but that it was concerned Israel would find a way to avoid carrying out the agreement. “Hamas did everything it could to deliver a deal based on reciprocity and simultaneous implementation,” he said. “Still, there are fears Israel could obstruct it.”



Efron said it was possible Israel and Hamas could soon return to “a familiar blame game”, accusing each other of failing to uphold the agreement announced by Trump while little change happens on the ground. This article originally appeared in The New York Times. Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: FIFA scraps World Cup sell-off plans, Infantino says
World.content:
Breaking SportSoccerFIFA World Cup FIFA scraps World Cup sell-off plans, Infantino says Updated August 1, 2026 — 9:51am ,first published 9:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

FIFA president Gianni Infantino said world soccer’s governing body has scrapped plans to sell a stake in the World Cup to private investors after widespread backlash. “Having listened carefully to all the views, it has become clear that the project has created divisions of a nature that, regardless of the level of support, are no longer in the interest of the objective set out in the first place,” Infantino said. FIFA President Gianni Infantino Getty Images Infantino’s confirmation came as one of his senior adviser’s quit in protest at plans to sell a stake in the World Cup as European football threatened a boycott and regional confederations united in opposition to the proposal. FIFA had proposed creating a $US 20-billion subsidiary, FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE), to run the World Cup and its other events, with a stake of up to 20 per cent to be offered to external investors. The senior adviser, Carlos Cordeiro, resigned with immediate effect, calling the plan “a bad deal for football”.



Cordeiro, who was appointed in 2021 by Infantino to help shape FIFA’s future, said the body was “mortgaging football’s future without any compelling justification. “It is a bad deal for FIFA’s Member Associations, a bad deal for football, and a bad deal for the long-term future of the game,” Cordeiro said. A former banker and ex-US Soccer Federation vice president, Cordeiro added that he had no involvement in the proposal and opposed it “unequivocally”. Meanwhile, FIFA’s chief operating officer Kevin Lamour said staff were “deceived” by Infantino, describing the proposal as a “project of one person”. “Our mission ... is to serve football. Not to serve the personal interests of a person who, unfortunately, believes he embodies FIFA when he is supposed to be at its service,” he wrote in a statement shared with the Associated Press.



FIFA had planned to proceed Despite opposition, Switzerland-based FIFA had previously said “incorrect media reports” this week had disrupted its planned consultation process but it would press on with the proposal to be considered by the 211 national football associations. Thrive Eternal, a fund run by Thrive Capital, founded by Joshua Kushner, was expected to lead the proposed investor group, FIFA said. Joshua is the brother of Jared Kushner, US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law. Trump, however, said he did not speak with Infantino about FIFA offering stakes to external investors despite having a close relationship after the US co-hosted the World Cup. British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who was critical of FIFA’s plan when it was announced earlier this week, told reporters on Friday that Infantino was “the wrong man to lead the organisation”.



Infantino, 56, is up for re-election next year and North American football chief Victor Montagliani is reportedly looking to challenge him. UEFA led opposition to FIFA plan European soccer’s governing body, UEFA, has led the opposition to the proposal, accusing FIFA of putting the sport’s “soul” up for sale. On Thursday, UEFA’s 55 member nations voted unanimously to boycott all FIFA tournaments, less than two weeks after Spain were crowned world champions. FIFA’s next major event is the women’s Under-20 World Cup in September. Hosts Poland said on Friday they had not received any information about the potential withdrawal of any team from the

tournament.



“Nobody is selling football. This is not something FIFA would ever entertain,” FIFA said in Friday’s statement. “Everyone has the right to express their opposition and to seek further clarification but no single entity can claim to represent all 211 MAs (member associations) around the world. “Each MA should be allowed to review the proposal and have a say in shaping their own future. These are the democratic principles of FIFA.” South American soccer governing body CONMEBOL said on Friday it had requested more information from FIFA on the proposal. “We recognise that the development of football requires commercial and financial decisions. However, such decisions must always serve football and never take precedence over its very

essence,” CONMEBOL said in a statement.



Related Article Analysis

FIFA World Cup FIFA’s offering Australia $45m to back selling the World Cup. Saying no might not be easy CONCACAF, the regional federation for North America, Central America and the Caribbean, rejected the proposal during a meeting on Thursday but the 41-member body did not follow UEFA with a boycott threat. The Asian Football Confederation, which has 47 members, issued a statement on Friday saying it “stands in solidarity” with UEFA and CONCACAF, but also stopped short of threatening a

boycott. The AFC, which has not historically been as frequent or vehement a critic of FIFA as its European counterpart UEFA, questioned the viability of the proposal and raised doubts about FIFA’s decision-making processes. Stuart Dykes, the director of European and Institutional Affairs at Football Supporters Europe, said such decisions could not be taken behind closed doors by a small group of people.



“The national associations should be demanding proper governance, proper consultation, proper stakeholder involvement,” Dykes told Reuters. “Football is not for sale. It’s a social good. Its value is created by the fans and the players ... That value is not for FIFA to extract in the interest of private investors.” FIFA says process is a democratic one Infantino said in a letter to all member associations that they would receive $40 million each if they agreed to FIFA’s proposal by September 19. On Friday, FIFA said it would not proceed with the plan without the support of the majority of its member associations.



“These principles underpin the FFE proposal: unprecedented development funding, truly global ownership of the commercial opportunities of our sport, and full self-determination through a democratic process for all MAs,” FIFA said. UEFA, CONCACAF and the AFC combined have 143 associations. However, not all individual member nations are certain to follow their federation’s line. The Czech FA’s President David Trunda told Sky Sports he could see the “positive impact of FIFA’s intentions”, but it has since rejected the proposal while endorsing UEFA’s stance. The Mexican Football Federation said it would study the proposal before deciding its position. Reuters
